A `[ThreadStatic]` reference-equality guard on the value being decoded lets a decoder call `mapper.Deserialize(...)` on the same BsonValue to reach the default materialisation without re-entering itself; nested documents (different BsonValue instances) still dispatch normally. No API, defaults, or exception paths changed — the pre-existing `DataTypeNotAssignable` check still runs first, so an unassignable discriminator throws before any callback.

The code path does not depend on that, so it works, but the regression net does not cover ctor-only/record types. (2) The fix is deserialization-only; the serializer side was already polymorphic via the pre-existing `_customSerializer.TryGetValue(obj.GetType())` fallback (since 2018), so the issue title's "serialization" half is fine but untested here. overshoot: Small. Behaviour does change for anyone who registered a decoder for a derived type and was (knowingly or not) getting default materialisation when loading through a base-typed collection — they now get the decoder's output. The re-entrancy guard is a `static [ThreadStatic]` field shared by every `BsonMapper` instance on the thread, including `BsonMapper.Global`: a decoder on mapper A that hands the same BsonValue to mapper B will have B's resolved decoder suppressed, and a decoder that resumes on a different thread (async-over-sync) would restore the guard onto an unrelated thread. No working path starts throwing, no new API, no default change, no measurable cost. Two small notes: the exception type on that path changes from NullReferenceException to LiteException (only breaks someone catching NRE specifically — not a real concern); and the guard sits after `if (item == null) continue;`, so an empty or all-null DbRef list on a type with no mapped _id still serializes, which is inconsistent with the single-ref path (RegisterDbRefItem throws for any non-null value) but preserves prior behaviour. Test-side, `Invalid_reference_later_in_insert_batch_rolls_back_earlier_rows` pins implicit-transaction rollback semantics for batch `Insert` that the report never raised — an assertion about unrelated engine behaviour that could become a brittle constraint later.
reporterNeed: Reporter (LiteDB 5.0.12, .NET 4.5) had an entity with a `[BsonRef]` collection/list of an interface type that has no mapped `_id`. Saving it blew up with an uncaught, undiagnosable exception instead of a LiteDB error. They diagnosed it themselves: the `#768` guard `if (idField == null) throw new LiteException(0, "There is no _id field mapped in your type: ...")` was added to `RegisterDbRefItem` in 5.0.12 but never to the list/array serializer `RegisterDbRefList`, so `idField.Getter(item)` NREs there. Their ask was literally "put that same check in the list path so I get a LiteException that names the type".
suggestedAction: Nothing required. Optional: when #2893 is closed, note on 2243 that the missing guard in `RegisterDbRefList` is now in place (BsonMapper.cs:331) so the reporter sees their own diagnosis was adopted verbatim.
whatChanged: Exactly the one line the reporter asked for, at LiteDB/Client/Mapper/BsonMapper.cs:331 inside `RegisterDbRefList`'s serializer: `if (idField == null) throw new LiteException(0, "There is no _id field mapped in your type: " + member.UnderlyingType.FullName);` placed immediately before `idField.Getter(item)`, mirroring the existing guard at line 259 in `RegisterDbRefItem` (using the element type instead of the member type). Plus two test files. The issue itself was closed as a duplicate of #2893, which is where the fix was tracked.

gap: No documentation was updated, which was the reporter's literal title and stated alternative ("a docs update would suffice"); the LiteDB wiki still does not state the rule. Also the sibling validation for index names (LiteDB/Engine/Engine/Index.cs:54 and :144) still throws the old, equally opaque "Use only [a-Z$_]" text, so a user hitting the same rule via EnsureIndex is still left guessing. Minor: the new message is emitted for every IsWord() failure, so a name like "my-collection" (hyphen, space, dot) now leads with "Names cannot start with a digit", which is not that name's actual cause — the trailing character list still points them right, but the headline is wrong for those inputs.
issueTitle: [BUG] Doc update request
overshoot: Essentially none on the production side: one string literal changed, no new API, no new exception path, no default or validation change, no perf cost. Test-side only: Issue2746_Tests pins the message with a regex requiring the wording to state the initial-digit/initial-letter rule (it does allow several phrasings), and the second test adds a TempFile + Checkpoint + reopen durability assertion (data written before and after the rejection survives a reopen) that the report never raised. reporterNeed: On v5.0.21 they passed a GUID-derived collection name ("2e4e2069_da7c_4dbd_8c11_a5ac31041079") to database.GetCollection<T>(name) and got "Invalid collection name '...': Use only [a-Z$_]." That message does not say the real rule — the name only contains characters from that set; the problem is that it starts with a digit. They spent time discovering the rule themselves and asked for either a clearer error or the rule to be documented. They did not ask for digit-leading names to be allowed.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2746 with the new message text so the reporter knows their exact ask landed, and state the rule plainly for them (first character must be a letter or underscore; digits, underscores and $ allowed afterwards; leading $ reserved) plus the practical workaround for GUID-named collections (prefix a letter, e.g. "c" + guid.ToString("N")). Then open a small follow-up issue to (a) add the naming rule to the wiki/docs, since the issue title was literally a doc request, and (b) give Index.cs:54/:144 the same explanatory message instead of "Use only [a-Z$_]".
whatChanged: CollectionService.CheckName's IsWord() failure message changed from "Use only [a-Z$_]" to "Names cannot start with a digit; use letters, digits, underscores or dollar signs (initial dollar signs are reserved)". That is accurate against Tokenizer.IsWordChar (first char: letter/_/$; later: letter/digit/_/$) and against the following StartsWith("$") check. Running the reporter's code now yields "Invalid collection name '2e4e2069_da7c_4dbd_8c11_a5ac31041079': Names cannot start with a digit; ..." — the rule they had to reverse-engineer is now in the message. The restriction itself is unchanged (still thrown at first write, when the collection is created, not at GetCollection()).

issueTitle: [BUG] [Crash / unchecked exception] Non-Int32-backed enums can abort serialization with EnumAsInteger=true
reporterNeed: With `EnumAsInteger = true`, `BsonMapper.Serialize` did `new BsonValue((int)obj)` (confirmed at their commit 61fa785a), which is an unbox-to-Int32 and throws `InvalidCastException` for byte-backed and long-backed enums. They want every CLR enum backing type (sbyte/byte/short/ushort/int/uint/long/ulong) to serialize without crashing, going through the declared underlying type rather than a direct Int32 unbox.
whatChanged: Serialize now reads `Enum.GetUnderlyingType`: ulong -> `unchecked((Int64)Convert.ToUInt64(obj))` (the same signed bit-pattern convention LiteDB already uses for raw `UInt64`), long/uint -> `Convert.ToInt64`, everything else -> `Convert.ToInt32`. Deserialize switched from `Enum.ToObject(type, value.AsInt32)` to reading `AsInt64` and converting through the underlying type (`unchecked((UInt64)number)` for ulong enums, `Convert.ChangeType` otherwise). Note the `InvalidCastException` itself had already been removed on dev by the earlier #2376 fix (e8d9b3755, `Convert.ToInt32(obj)`); this commit removes the remaining width loss (Convert.ToInt32 overflow / silent truncation) for long, uint and ulong enums.
gap: None for the reported scenario. Byte-backed and long-backed enums round-trip with EnumAsInteger=true; the theory test covers all eight backing types plus an insert/reopen/index/query round trip.
overshoot: Three things go beyond the report. (1) Deserialize is now strict: a stored integer outside the backing type throws `OverflowException` where `Enum.ToObject` used to truncate silently (e.g. 300 into a `byte`-backed enum used to yield 44), and this is pinned by `Stored_integers_outside_the_backing_type_throw_instead_of_truncating`. The exception is a bare `Convert` message ("Value was either too large or too small for...") naming neither the field, the document, nor the enum type, so anyone who hits it on legacy or hand-written data gets no actionable hint. Only reachable with mismatched/hand-authored data (old code threw OverflowException for anything outside Int32 anyway), so blast radius is small but real, and stricter reading was not requested. (2) Stored BSON type for long-, uint- and ulong-backed enums changes from Int32 to Int64 for values that used to fit. Cross-type numeric comparison in `BsonValue.CompareTo` (decimal promotion) means existing Int32 documents and indexes still match Int64 queries, so this is not a break, but raw-document consumers checking `IsInt32` will see the change. (3) ulong enum values >= 2^63 are now storable but stored as negative Int64, so they sort below small values in indexes and range queries; equality is correct (the test only asserts equality). Consistent with LiteDB's existing raw-UInt64 handling, so defensible, but it is new silently-misordering data that previously could not be written at all.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2769 confirming the mapping rule now used (ulong -> unchecked signed Int64 bit pattern, long/uint -> Int64, rest -> Int32) and flagging the two side effects a user should know: long/uint/ulong enums now serialize as BSON Int64 instead of Int32 (queries still match across both), and ulong values above Int64.MaxValue store as negative so they do not sort correctly. Optionally a small follow-up to include the enum type and stored value in the new OverflowException message, since as written it gives no clue which property failed.

issueTitle: LiteDB.Shell ignores absolute Unix paths (arguments starting with / are parsed as options)
reporterNeed: Reporter (the maintainer himself, on Linux, dev 6.x prerelease 47268cb4) ran `dotnet LiteDB.Shell.dll /home/me/data/app.db` and no database opened and no error was printed: `OptionSet.Parse` matched `^(--|-|\/)(\w+)`, read `/home/...` as an unregistered option named `home`, and dropped it. He wanted an absolute Unix path to open the database like any other path, without the `--exec "open ..."` workaround.
whatChanged: `LiteDB.Shell/Utils/OptionSet.cs` now picks the option-prefix regex at runtime: `^(--|-|\/)` on Windows, `^(--|-)` elsewhere. On Linux/macOS `/home/me/data/app.db` no longer matches, so it falls to the `_extra_` branch, which `Program.cs` maps to `open <path>`. The reporter's exact command line now opens the database. Windows behaviour (`/pretty` etc.) is untouched. 5 added / 1 removed line, no other file.
gap: No automated test. `OptionSet` is internal to the LiteDB.Shell exe and no test project references that project (grep: `OptionSet` appears only in `Program.cs` and `OptionSet.cs`; nothing in `LiteDB.Tests` touches the shell), so nothing in CI would catch a regression here — the PR body cites only manual real-process probes. Also untouched: the issue's side note that `LiteDB.Shell/Properties/launchSettings.json` hardcodes `commandLineArgs: "app.db"`, so a bare `dotnet run` still silently opens/creates `app.db` in the working directory. The broader "silently ignores" root cause is also still there: an unregistered option is still skipped with a bare `continue` (OptionSet.cs:67) and no message — only the `/path` symptom was removed.
overshoot: Minor, and deliberate: on non-Windows the Windows-style switch form is now gone entirely, so `/pretty`, `/exit`, `/run script.txt`, `/exec "..."` stop being options on Linux/macOS. `/run x.txt` in particular now silently becomes `open /run` instead of running the script — a silent behaviour flip for anyone who scripted that form on Unix. The reporter's own suggested alternative ("only when `x` is a registered option name, and fall back to the path handler otherwise") would have fixed `/home/...` without removing those. No new public API, no new exceptions, no default change on Windows, negligible cost (one `RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform` per `Parse` call). It is listed in the PR release notes.
suggestedAction: Nothing blocking. Optionally a small follow-up issue for the two leftovers the report itself names: the hardcoded `app.db` in `LiteDB.Shell/Properties/launchSettings.json`, and unregistered options being dropped silently instead of producing a message. If shell behaviour is worth protecting, a tiny test project over `OptionSet` (make it `public` or add `InternalsVisibleTo`) would pin the Unix-path case that currently rests on a one-off manual probe.

issueTitle: Overridden BsonMapper.ToObject is never called when reading through ILiteCollection<T> / ILiteQueryable<T> in v5
reporterNeed: #2802 is a maintainer-written consolidation of two real reports: humhei (#1977, 5.0.10) subclassed BsonMapper and overrode both `ToObject(Type, BsonDocument)` and `ToObject<T>(BsonDocument)` to throw — reads completed normally, so the overrides were provably never invoked (repro project humhei/LiteDBCustomBsonMapper); and vshapenko (#1366) upgraded an F# app from v4 to v5 and found his custom mapper "completely ignored", which broke his types that have no default constructor. Both needed the mapper-wide read hook to actually run on `FindAll`/`Find`/`FindById`/`FindOne`/`Query().ToList()`, as it did in v4.
whatChanged: One production line: in `LiteQueryable.ToEnumerable()` the non-simple-type branch now maps rows with `_mapper.ToObject<T>(x)` instead of `(T)_mapper.Deserialize(typeof(T), x)`. Every typed read funnels through this method — `LiteCollection<T>.Find/FindById/FindOne/FindAll` all build on `Query()`, and `LiteRepository` delegates to those — so all five APIs named in the reports now dispatch through the virtual hook, and the object the override returns is the object handed back. The `_isSimpleType` branch keeps `Deserialize`, as the issue asked. At the parent commit `ToObject(Type, BsonDocument)` was just a null guard plus a `BsonDocument` short-circuit in front of `Deserialize`, so for the default mapper the mapping result is unchanged.
gap: Small and inherent to the fix, not a leftover blocker. (1) The hook fires for the root entity only; nested members and collection elements still go through `Deserialize`, so an F# user whose *fields* are no-default-ctor records/unions still needs `RegisterType<T>` or a `Deserialize` override — `Deserialize(Type, BsonValue)` is already virtual, but nothing tells the reporter that. (2) `GetCollection<BsonDocument>` and scalar/`_isSimpleType` projections deliberately still bypass `ToObject`; correct, but undocumented, so a reporter testing with those shapes would think it is still broken. Neither reporter has been told any of this — #1977 and #1366 were closed as duplicates pointing at #2802, and #2802 carries no "fixed, here is what works now" comment.
overshoot: Nothing material in merged dev. No new public API, no changed defaults, no stricter validation on a working path (the added `ArgumentNullException` for a null doc is unreachable on this branch, and replaces a NullReferenceException), cost is one extra virtual call and cast per row. The commit did introduce one self-inflicted regression: with `T == BsonDocument`, `ToObject` returns the document unchanged and so skipped `OnDeserialization` callbacks that `Deserialize` used to fire. That was fixed 26 minutes later by 79a48cc82 ("Preserve raw document deserialization callbacks") in the same PR, which re-added an explicit `typeof(T) == typeof(BsonDocument)` branch — so it never reached dev, but the fix commit read on its own is incomplete. The tests pin `Reads == 1`, i.e. exactly one hook call per row; that is what the report asks for, not an over-specification.
suggestedAction: Comment once on #2802 (and, since both original reporters were redirected there, @-mention humhei and vshapenko) stating: overriding either `ToObject(Type, BsonDocument)` or `ToObject<T>(BsonDocument)` is now invoked exactly once per row on FindAll/Find/FindById/FindOne/Query, and the object the override returns is the one returned to the caller; and name the deliberate scope — root entity only, nested/element types go through the (virtual) `Deserialize` or `RegisterType<T>`, and raw `BsonDocument` collections plus scalar projections bypass `ToObject` by design. Ship it in the release notes as "typed reads call the virtual BsonMapper.ToObject once per row" (already drafted in the PR body).

gap: End-to-end, no LongCount overload can actually return a value above int.MaxValue: the aggregate COUNT is `values.Count()` (Enumerable.Count(), int-returning) in LiteDB/Document/Expression/Methods/Aggregate.cs:18, so the engine overflows before the Int64 reader is reached. The reporter's scoped complaint (delegation inconsistency) is fixed, but the long-count family remains theoretical past 2^31 documents. That limitation is pre-existing and shared by LongCount(), LongCount(BsonExpression) and the LINQ overloads, so it is outside this report.
issueTitle: LongCount(Query) counts through the int Count() path, so it can't exceed int.MaxValue
overshoot: Production side: none — one line, no new API, no new exceptions, no default or perf change, Count(Query) untouched. Test side, mild: Issue2839_Tests.cs pins internals the report does not justify — the literal `{ count: COUNT(*._id) }` select source, Includes empty, GroupBy/Having null, ForUpdate/ExplainPlan false, and exact Offset 17 / Limit 23 round-trip — so unrelated refactors of the count pipeline will fail it. It is also gated `#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER` (DispatchProxy), so net4x builds get no coverage.
reporterNeed: The reporter (the maintainer, from an API review in #2837, not from user data) found that ILiteCollection<T>.LongCount(Query) delegated to LiteQueryable<T>.Count(), which reads the result via .AsInt32, so the long overload could never exceed int.MaxValue while every sibling LongCount overload was correct. He wanted the overload made consistent and the delegation pinned by a test, since building a 2^31-document collection in CI is impractical.
suggestedAction: Nothing required for #2839. Optionally file a separate follow-up noting that BsonExpressionMethods.COUNT uses Enumerable.Count() (int), which caps every LongCount overload below 2^31 regardless of the client-side Int64 reader — that is the only remaining honest caveat.
whatChanged: LiteDB/Client/Database/Collections/Aggregate.cs:91 now calls new LiteQueryable<T>(...).LongCount() instead of .Count(). The two LiteQueryable methods are identical apart from .AsInt64 vs .AsInt32 (LiteQueryable.cs:411-446), so query, filtering, ordering, offset/limit and select restoration are unchanged. The test uses a DispatchProxy fake ILiteEngine that returns 4,294,967,303 for the filtered route and asserts LongCount(query) returns it exactly, with distinct per-route results so the implementation cannot pass by ignoring the supplied Query.

issueTitle: After a fatal ENSURE error, DropCollection/RenameCollection/Pragma report "open transaction" instead of the real error
reporterNeed: Reporter (the maintainer, self-filed, no comments) hit a closed engine after a fatal INVALID_DATAFILE_STATE/IOException: the failing thread keeps a leaked read lock, so DropCollection/RenameCollection/Pragma(set) on that thread report error 126 "thread already contains an open transaction" instead of the real 999 error — which sends users hunting for a missing Commit/Rollback in their own code and, in a loop (#2545), hides the original failure entirely. He wanted those three entry points to call _state.Validate() before the IsInTransaction check, and optionally the lock released on close.
whatChanged: _state.Validate() is now the first real check in LiteEngine.DropCollection and RenameCollection (before `if (_locker.IsInTransaction)`), and in the Pragma(string) getter — which also covers the Pragma(string, BsonValue) setter, since the setter's first statement is `this.Pragma(name)`. Validate() rethrows the stored original exception, so the reporter's repro now prints 999 "Page type must be data page" for every follow-up call instead of 126. No lock-release change.
gap: The optional half of the report is not done: the failing thread still holds the read lock, ReaderWriterLockSlim.Dispose still throws and is swallowed in LockService, so LockService is never really disposed and IsInTransaction stays true for that thread for the engine's lifetime. Harmless now that every metadata entry point validates first, but the leak the reporter described remains. Also unchanged: GetCollectionNames() (Collection.cs:14) still reads _header directly with no Validate, so it silently returns stale names on a closed/disposed engine — the reporter did not list it, but it is the same class of bug.
overshoot: Validate() was added to the Pragma *read* path, which the report did not ask for, and the new test pins it (`db.Pragma("TIMEOUT")` after Dispose must throw ENGINE_DISPOSED). Two consequences other users pay for: (1) any pragma read after Dispose — db.UserVersion, db.Collation, db.CheckpointSize, db.Timeout, db.LimitSize, all of which previously returned the cached header value — now throws LiteException ENGINE_DISPOSED; (2) concrete regression: LiteDatabase.Dispose has no idempotency guard (LiteDatabase.cs:394-405) and _checkpointOverride is a readonly field that is never cleared, so for a stream-constructed LiteDatabase with a checkpoint override, a second Dispose() now calls _engine.Pragma(CHECKPOINT, override) -> Pragma(name) -> Validate() -> throws ENGINE_DISPOSED, where before it compared equal and returned false silently. Double-dispose (using + explicit Dispose, DI containers) is legal and now throws from Dispose.
suggestedAction: Follow-up issue: make LiteDatabase.Dispose idempotent (a _disposed guard, or skip the checkpoint restore when the engine is already closed) so the new Pragma-read validation cannot make a second Dispose throw; optionally add Validate() to GetCollectionNames and file the leaked-lock release (report's "optional" item) as its own issue. Nothing to tell the reporter — their scenario is fixed.

issueTitle: LiteDB.Shell spins forever at end of piped input when the last command has no trailing semicolon
reporterNeed: Reporter (JKamsker himself, self-filed, 0 comments) pipes commands into LiteDB.Shell from a script/CI job; if the last SQL command lacks a trailing `;`, the process never exits, burns 100% CPU and floods stdout with `| ` continuation prompts (~300 KB in 8 s). He needed the shell to terminate at EOF instead of hanging, explicitly leaving open whether the unterminated command should be executed or reported as incomplete.
whatChanged: In LiteDB.Shell/Shell/InputCommand.cs: the multi-line continuation loop now checks `ReadLine() == null` and, on EOF, sets AutoExit/Running=false and returns "exit" (discarding the unfinished SQL); the EOF-on-first-line branch returns "exit" instead of "" so the Quit command runs and disposes the database; and `ReadLine()` returns null instead of the literal string "exit" when AutoExit is set. Tracing the repro: `open t.db` executes, then `select $ from $database` enters the loop, ReadLine returns null at EOF, ReadCommand returns "exit", ShellProgram dispatches Quit (disposes DB, Running=false) and the while loop ends. The old `if (AutoExit) return "exit"` also made `--exec "<sql without ;>" --exit` loop forever appending "exit"; that path now terminates too.
gap: No test at all: the commit touches only InputCommand.cs, there is no shell test project, and LiteDB.Tests references nothing from LiteDB.Shell. The PR body admits the three shell commits were "read only", verified by out-of-band real-process probes that are not in CI — so the hang can regress silently, and the reporter's own suggestion (give InputCommand a TextReader so this is a plain unit test) was not taken. Behaviourally, the commit picks neither of the two options the report named: the unterminated trailing command is silently discarded — no message, no non-zero exit code. A CI job that forgets one `;` now exits 0 with its last command never run, which is quieter than a hang but still gives the script author nothing to go on. Cosmetically, one stray `| ` is still written before the EOF check.
overshoot: Essentially none. Three lines of a console exe, no library/public API surface, no new exception, no default or perf change. Two small unrequested extras, both benign and arguably necessary: EOF at a command boundary now returns "exit" instead of "", so Quit runs and disposes the database (previously the process just fell out of the loop undisposed); and the AutoExit-with-unterminated-queued-SQL loop is fixed as a side effect. One trivial side effect: the synthetic "exit" is no longer appended to InputCommand.History, which only the interactive `ed` command reads.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2843 stating the decision explicitly ("an unterminated last command at EOF is discarded, not executed"), since the report left that open; and open a follow-up to (a) print an "incomplete command discarded" warning to stderr, preferably with a non-zero exit code so piped CI jobs notice, and (b) add the regression test the report asked for by letting InputCommand take a TextReader.

gap: Non-finite doubles are still written as `null` and read back as `BsonType.Null` — the same silent value+type loss the report describes, for NaN/±Infinity instead of MaxValue. The issue asked to "decide on a representation ... or at least document the current behaviour"; the commit decides (keep `null`) and pins it with a test, but adds no user-visible documentation (no XML doc, no docs change) and nothing was said on #2845 or on the downstream user issue #2328, which is still open awaiting the reporter's read-back method. So a user whose computed double becomes Infinity still loses it on JSON export with no warning and no place that says so.
issueTitle: JsonSerializer doesn't round-trip doubles: ~15 significant digits, double.MaxValue becomes Infinity, then null
overshoot:
Two items beyond the report, neither fatal:
1. Negative zero. The report never mentions it. `JsonReader` now reconstructs -0.0 from any token that parses to 0 and starts with '-' ("-0", "-0.0", "-0E+20"), and `JsonWriter` force-writes "-0.0". On .NET Core this was already the behaviour, but on netstandard2.0/.NET Framework a JSON "-0" that previously became +0.0 now stores negative zero — and `BsonValue.CompareTo` (BsonValue.cs:590) uses `double.CompareTo`, where -0.0 < 0.0, so such a document no longer compares/indexes equal to 0. A new test (`Json_reader_preserves_explicit_negative_zero`) pins this expectation, which the report does not justify.
2. Cost on every JSON double. `FormatDouble` does `ToString("R")` plus a verifying `double.TryParse` for every double written. The verification only earns its keep on netstandard2.0-on-Framework (where "R" is unreliable); on net8.0/net10.0 "R" is already shortest-round-trip, so the extra parse is pure overhead paid by everyone serializing JSON. It could be `#if`-gated to netstandard2.0.
3. (Expected, not really overshoot) JSON text changes globally: exponent notation now appears for very small/large values (`1E-07`, `1E+21`). LiteDB's own tokenizer handles it (Tokenizer.cs:592-616) and the PR release notes call it out.
reporterNeed: Reporter (the maintainer, filing on behalf of user issue #2328) needs a BsonDocument's doubles to survive a JSON round trip unchanged: `double.MaxValue` came back as `Infinity` after one pass and as `BsonType.Null` after a second, and `0.1 + 0.2` came back as `0.3`, so export/import, `ToString()`+parse and anything that displays documents as JSON (LiteDB Studio) silently altered values that the BSON path stores exactly.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2845 (and on #2328) stating the decision plainly: finite doubles now round-trip bit-exactly through JSON, exponent notation appears for very small/large values, and NaN/±Infinity are deliberately still written as `null` (so they come back as `BsonType.Null`) — with a one-line XML-doc/docs note on JsonSerializer/JsonWriter saying so, since the issue accepted "at least document the current behaviour". Optionally gate the `FormatDouble` verify-parse to netstandard2.0, and double-check the unrequested negative-zero reader rule against index/equality behaviour before it ships.
whatChanged: `JsonWriter` replaces the lossy `ToString("0.0########")` (≈15 significant digits, max 9 decimals) with `FormatDouble`: `"R"`, verified by re-parsing and comparing bits, falling back to `G17` — plus a `.0` suffix when the text has no '.' or exponent so the token still deserialises as Double rather than Int32/Int64, and an explicit "-0.0" for negative zero. `JsonReader` reconstructs negative zero on runtimes that normalise it away. Result: `double.MaxValue` → `1.7976931348623157E+308` and back exactly; `0.1+0.2` → `0.30000000000000004`; three consecutive round trips keep bits and `BsonType.Double`. Tests cover exactly the list the issue asked for (MaxValue, MinValue, Epsilon, 0.1+0.2, 1e-300) with bit-level assertions, repeated exports, a de-DE culture run over 2000 random finite bit patterns, and the readable-text expectation (`0.1` stays `0.1`, not `0.10000000000000001`).

gap: Two culture-sensitive `.ToLower()` calls remain that still misbehave under tr-TR, both outside what the issue names: `LiteDB/Document/Expression/Methods/Date.cs:92` and `:116` lowercase the date-part argument, so `DATEADD('MINUTE', ...)` / `DATEDIFF('MIN...')` with any uppercase `I` become "mınute" and silently return `BsonValue.Null` instead of a value or an error. (`Query.cs:74` `IntoAutoId.ToString().ToLower()` also yields "ınt32", but only in log/diagnostic SQL text, never re-parsed; `JsonReader.cs:97` and `DictionaryExtensions.cs:234` handle only tokens without `i`/`I`, so they are safe.) Everything the issue itself asked for is covered; the tokenizer keyword set and all secondary keyword matching already use `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`, so no further SQL-parsing path is culture-dependent.
issueTitle: SQL parser uses culture-sensitive ToUpper(): lowercase keywords fail to parse under tr-TR
overshoot: Production change is minimal and risk-free: 5 lines, `ToUpper()` → `ToUpperInvariant()`, no new API, no new exception path, no behaviour change outside tr/az cultures, no perf cost. Only test-level overreach: `AssertRebuiltState` (Issue2858_Tests.cs:129-143) pins REBUILD semantics the report never mentions — collation persistence to `en-US/None`, `UserVersion` survival, unique-index preservation, and case-sensitivity of the rebuilt collation. If rebuild collation semantics are deliberately changed later, this test fails under a #2858 label that has nothing to do with the cause. Also, the guard assertions at lines 202-205 (`"insert".ToUpper() == "İNSERT"`) will hard-fail rather than skip if the suite is ever run with InvariantGlobalization enabled (not set anywhere today).
reporterNeed: The issue is maintainer-filed (JKamsker), consolidating a downstream need: Strange Loop Games / gzatravkin ship a LiteDB fork because on machines running under Turkish culture (`tr-TR`) lowercase SQL keywords do not parse — `"insert".ToUpper()` yields `İNSERT`, so `insert into …`, `rebuild …`, `commit` and the `:int` auto-id suffix all throw `UnexpectedToken`. No comments, no other reporters, still OPEN.
suggestedAction: Comment on the issue and close it, answering all three bullets honestly: (1) the non-generic IDictionary crash was fixed in v5; this commit closes the remaining variants (a generic type with fewer/differently-ordered type arguments implementing IDictionary, e.g. `class Foo<T> : Hashtable` or `class Foo<T> : Dictionary<string,int>`, which still threw IndexOutOfRange), and dictionary key/value types are now taken from the implemented dictionary contract; (2) delegates and MemberInfo (including System.Type) now serialize to Null so an Exception serializes with its Message/Data/InnerException intact — and note that SerializeObject can be overridden, or RegisterType used, to emit a representation instead of Null; (3) no new FromObject/ToObject(BsonValue) is needed — use `mapper.Serialize<T>(value)` / `Serialize(Type, object)` which return BsonValue, and `mapper.Deserialize<T>(BsonValue)` / `Deserialize(Type, BsonValue)`; both have been public since v5. Separately, consider documenting (release notes) that `Type`/delegate/MemberInfo members now serialize as Null rather than a junk document, since that is silent and affects users who never filed this issue.
whatChanged: Serialize: a new branch before the type dispatch returns `SerializeObject(...) ?? BsonValue.Null` for `Delegate`/`MemberInfo`, and the base `SerializeObject` returns null for those — so an Exception's TargetSite no longer drags the mapper into the reflection graph (previously it recursed into MethodBase/Type members until MaxDepth), while RegisterType and a SerializeObject override still win. Dictionary key/value types now come from `Reflection.GetDictionaryTypes`, which derives the schema from the implemented dictionary contract (IDictionary interface map for concrete types, declared generic arguments for interfaces) instead of blindly taking `type.GetGenericArguments()[0]/[1]`; that removes the IndexOutOfRange for generic types with <2 or reordered arguments implementing IDictionary. Nothing was added for the ToObject/FromObject request.

issueTitle: Implicit BsonValue from ulong operator casts to double instead of long.
reporterNeed: The reporter stored entities keyed by a `ulong` and could not fetch them: `FindById(myUlong)` always returned null, because the implicit `ulong -> BsonValue` operator produced a Double while BsonMapper persisted the same `ulong` as an Int64. A second commenter (GreemDev) reported the mirror symptom — InvalidCastException when reading those values back into `ulong` (Int32/Double RawValue unboxed as UInt64).
whatChanged: `implicit operator BsonValue(UInt64)` now returns `new BsonValue(unchecked((Int64)value))` instead of `new BsonValue((Double)value)`, so a ulong literal/variable used as a query key produces exactly the same BsonType.Int64 bit pattern that BsonMapper writes for a `ulong` property. The reverse operator (Int64/Int32 -> ulong, unchecked) and the mapper side were already fixed upstream in #2898; this commit closes the last asymmetric direction. One assertion in Implicit_Tests was updated from IsDouble/AsDouble to IsInt64/(ulong) round-trip.
gap: Issue1224_Tests.Upper_half_UInt64_values_survive_typed_reopen_and_indexed_queries covers exactly the reporter's flow — POCO with `[BsonId] ulong`, insert, reopen, `records.FindById(someUlong)` and `Find(x => x.Value == someUlong)` — plus bit-level wire-byte checks. Remaining gap, not affecting the reporter: ulongs above Int64.MaxValue are stored as negative Int64, so equality works but ordering/range queries across the 2^63 boundary are numerically wrong (ulong.MaxValue sorts before 1); the test only asserts ordering among four upper-half values, where the signed order happens to coincide. Also, existing databases whose ulong fields were written through the old implicit operator hold Doubles: cross-type numeric comparison keeps them matchable below 2^53, but above that (and for anything > Int64.MaxValue) a ulong query silently stops finding them, and `(ulong)value` on such a stored Double still throws a bare InvalidCastException with no guidance — a behaviour the new test now pins as expected.
overshoot: Nothing beyond the minimum in production code (3 lines, no new API, no new exception path, no perf cost). Two knock-on effects worth a release note: every `BsonValue` built from a ulong changes type Double -> Int64, so code branching on IsDouble/AsDouble breaks, and JSON export of such fields changes from a plain number to extended `{"$numberLong":"..."}` (JsonWriter.cs:128). Both are required for consistency with BsonMapper, so this is not scope creep.
suggestedAction: Nothing blocking. When #2917 lands, add one release-note/changelog line: implicit ulong conversions now produce BSON Int64 (two's-complement) matching BsonMapper — documents that previously stored ulongs as Double via the implicit operator may no longer be found for values above 2^53, and ordering/range queries on ulongs above Int64.MaxValue remain signed. Optionally post that same note on #2898 so subscribers of the closed #1224 see it.

issueTitle: v5 Beta - NotSupportedException: Dictionary.ContainsKey()
overshoot:
The commit bundles a full Any/All quantifier rewrite for a different issue (#2810) into the same change: new `LinqExpressionVisitor.Quantifier.cs` (152 lines) and `LinqExpressionVisitor.References.cs` (81 lines), deletion of `VisitEnumerablePredicate` from the main visitor, a new `_dbRefType` assignment inside `ResolvePattern` that fires for every `@n` lambda argument (line 566), and `_lambdaReferences` bookkeeping around every lambda. None of that is needed for #1376 — a `ContainsKey` fix needs only `DictionaryResolver`, the `EnumerableResolver` line, and `CONTAINSKEY`. It also adds a new NotSupportedException ("Nested collection predicates cannot refer to an outer collection item.") and shifts quantifier lambdas that `CanUseDirectQuantifier` does not whitelist (only `# LIKE `/`# = ` patterns and simple comparisons) onto a `MAP(...) ANY = true` translation instead of the index-friendly `@0 ANY %` form.

New public BsonExpression function `CONTAINSKEY` plus two runtime throws (ArgumentNullException on a null key, NotSupportedException when the field is a non-null non-document) are new surface, but they sit only on paths that previously threw at translation time, so nothing that worked before now fails.
reporterNeed: UserR00T (BPEssentials) migrated from LiteDB v4 to v5 and could not run `Users.Find(x => x.Character.CustomData.Data.ContainsKey(CustomDataKey))`, where `Data` is a `Dictionary<string, object>` and `CustomDataKey` is a captured string property ("bpe:cooldowns"). LiteDB threw `NotSupportedException: Method ContainsKey() in Dictionary\`2 are not supported`. They wanted a server-side key-presence filter instead of loading every user and checking in a foreach.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1376 that `ContainsKey` on a string-keyed dictionary (and on `BsonDocument`) now translates to a new `CONTAINSKEY(...)` expression in v6/PR #2917, with the one caveat the reporter cannot guess: matching uses BSON field-name semantics (case-insensitive), so it can differ from in-memory `Dictionary.ContainsKey`, and the field must be stored as a document (an `IDictionary` that serialized as an array, e.g. `ExpandoObject`, throws). Separately, consider splitting the #2810 Any/All quantifier rewrite out of this commit so the #1376 fix can be reviewed and reverted independently.
whatChanged: `DictionaryResolver.IsContainsKey` identifies any instance `bool ContainsKey(string)` that is the `IDictionary<string,_>` / `IReadOnlyDictionary<string,_>` implementation (via `GetInterfaceMap`, so a `new`-hidden method is deliberately not matched), and `EnumerableResolver.ResolveMethod` maps it to `CONTAINSKEY(#, @0)`. `Dictionary<string,object>` reaches that resolver through `TryGetResolver` -> ICollectionResolver -> base EnumerableResolver. The new `BsonExpressionMethods.CONTAINSKEY(document, key)` returns `document.AsDocument.ContainsKey(key)`, treats a missing/null field as false, and distinguishes an absent key from a key whose value is null. So the reporter's `Find(x => x.Character.CustomData.Data.ContainsKey(CustomDataKey))` translates to `CONTAINSKEY($.Character.CustomData.Data, @p0)` and runs server-side. Tests cover the exact shape: `col.Find(x => x.Data.ContainsKey(key))` with a captured key over `Dictionary<string,object>`, plus negation, parameterized/odd keys, and `IDictionary`/`IReadOnlyDictionary` casts.

issueTitle: [SOLVED but...] Query.Limit is ignored by Find(Query)
reporterNeed: nightroman (LiteDB 5.0.3, net45) set `query.Limit = 1` on a hand-built `Query` and called `col.Find(query)`, but got all documents back. He then diagnosed the cause himself: `Find(Query, skip, limit)` unconditionally assigned its default parameters onto the caller's `Query`, wiping the caller's Offset/Limit. After the 2020 partial fix (`if (skip != 0) …`) he explicitly said it was still wrong: passing non-default skip/limit still mutates the caller's `Query`, so reusing that instance later silently pages differently. His preferred remedy was to drop the skip/limit parameters from `Find` altogether and let `Query` own paging.
whatChanged: In `LiteDB/Client/Database/Collections/Find.cs`, when `skip != 0 || limit != int.MaxValue`, `Find` now builds a private `Query` copy (Select, GroupBy, Having, ForUpdate, Vector*, Into/IntoAutoId, ExplainPlan, plus copied Includes/Where/OrderBy lists), applies the overrides to the copy, and executes that. The caller's `Query` is never written to — including during lazy enumeration. The no-override path is untouched, so `Find(query)` still honours `query.Limit`/`query.Offset` as before.
gap: The reporter's preferred fix — removing the `skip`/`limit` parameters from `Find(Query, …)` — is not done, and his design question ("why these two parameters and not Order? Find should take just Query") is still unanswered in the issue. That is a preference, not a defect: with the mutation gone, the parameters are now harmless per-call overrides. But nothing in the XML docs on `Find(Query, int, int)` / `ILiteCollection.Find` states that skip/limit are execution-local and do not modify the passed query, so a user still has to read the source or run the test to learn it.
overshoot: Small and mostly benign. (1) Behaviour change for anyone who (deliberately or accidentally) relied on `Find(q, skip, limit)` leaving the overrides on `q` for a later `Find(q)` — that is the point of the fix, but it is a silent semantic change for third parties, with no release note in the commit. (2) The copy is hand-rolled field-by-field with no `Query.Clone()` and no test asserting completeness; it currently matches every settable property on `Query` (verified against LiteDB/Engine/Query/Query.cs), but any new `Query` property added later — and this fork is actively adding vector properties — will be silently dropped on the override path only, producing a hard-to-find divergence between `Find(q)` and `Find(q, skip, limit)`. (3) One extra `Query` plus three list copies allocated per call when overrides are supplied; negligible. No new exceptions, no new public API, no changed defaults, no stricter validation. Test assertions stay within what the thread justifies (no mutation, query reusable, projection/include/order preserved).
suggestedAction: Comment on #1506 and close it: the original `Find(query)` ignoring `Query.Limit` was fixed in 5.0.x, and as of this commit non-default `skip`/`limit` no longer touch the caller's `Query` — they are applied to an internal copy, so the same `Query` instance can be reused safely, which is what nightroman asked for. Answer his remaining design question honestly: the parameters stay for source compatibility and are now defined as per-call overrides. Two cheap follow-ups: add that sentence to the XML doc on `Find(Query, int, int)` and `ILiteCollection.Find`; and replace the hand-rolled copy with a `Query` copy helper (or add a reflection-based test that every settable `Query` property is carried over) so the override path cannot silently drop a future property.

gap: The reporter's secondary ask (their follow-up comment: "only handle a few method for ICollection ... bring back the property access") is not addressed. The fix special-cases GroupingResolver only; any other resolver-owned type whose ResolveMember returns null still throws "Member X are not support in Y" even when the operand is a pure client-side capture (e.g. a captured DateTime's .Ticks / .DayOfWeek / .TimeOfDay, since DateTimeResolver.ResolveMember returns null for those). That failure is at least an explicit, member-named NotSupportedException, not silent wrong results, so the reporter can see what to hoist into a local — but they still have to hoist it manually.
issueTitle: [BUG]BsonExpression with IGrouping.Key acts an unexpect behavior
overshoot: None material. The new branch is gated on `!isParam && type is GroupingResolver`, i.e. only `.Key` reached through a captured (non-lambda-parameter) grouping — a path that previously produced wrong results anyway. Server-side grouping (`g => g.Key` where g IS the lambda parameter, incl. nested lambdas over it, since ParameterExpressionVisitor.Test is run on the sub-expression) still emits `@key`, and a test pins that. No new public API, no changed defaults, no new exception on a path that used to work, no cost paid by other queries (the compiled Evaluate only runs for captured grouping keys). Only nit: a captured grouping that is null now surfaces a NullReferenceException from the compiled delegate rather than a LiteDB-worded message — same as every other captured-constant path, so not a regression specific to this change.
reporterNeed: They iterate CLR groups (`foreach (var item in list.GroupBy(x => x.gid))`) and want to query LiteDB per group with `col.Find(x => x.gid == item.Key)`. The captured `item.Key` was not treated as a plain captured value, so the predicate could not be translated; their only workaround was to copy `item.Key` into a local before every Find, which they said is unworkable for complex predicates and silently bug-prone when someone uses `.Key` inline by accident.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1545: confirm the captured-IGrouping.Key case is fixed in PR #2917 (commit 70dbcbcab0) — `x => x.gid == item.Key` now binds the key as a query parameter, and note that before the fix it had degraded from an exception to silently returning no rows (it translated to `$.gid = @key`, an undefined BsonExpression parameter that evaluates to null). Also answer their second point honestly: the general "fall back to client-side evaluation whenever a resolver has no pattern for a captured member" change they proposed was not taken; only IGrouping.Key is special-cased, and other unsupported members on resolver-owned types (e.g. a captured DateTime's .Ticks/.DayOfWeek) still throw NotSupportedException naming the member. Invite a separate issue if they hit one of those.
whatChanged: In LinqExpressionVisitor.VisitMember, when a member access is NOT rooted in the query's lambda parameter and its declaring type resolves to GroupingResolver, the node is now compiled and evaluated and emitted as a BsonExpression parameter (`@p0`) instead of the server-side `@key` token. For the reporter's loop this makes `col.Find(x => x.gid == item.Key)` translate to `$.gid = @p0` with p0 = the current group key, and it re-evaluates per call because BsonMapper.GetExpression builds a fresh visitor each time (no expression cache), so a reused Expression<Func<..>> also picks up the current capture. Composite keys (`group.Key.Number`) work because the existing _memberAccessNodes stack is still applied in VisitConstant.

gap: The remaining cost that commenter holyping actually named is untouched: `Query.Compose` still renders both operands back to text, concatenates, and re-parses the whole growing string on every call (LiteDB/Client/Structures/Query.Composition.cs:9-19), and `Query.Or(params ...)` folds pairwise, so composition stays O(n^2) in parse/allocation. For n=100 that is now tens of ms instead of 2503 ms, but a user chaining thousands of terms is still quadratic, and 4.1.4's 2 ms is not restored. The big compile is also not eliminated, only moved: the first `Find`/`ExecuteScalar` on the finished 100-term expression pays it. Neither point is stated anywhere the reporter can see, and no test bounds the cost, so a future change could silently reintroduce eager compilation.
issueTitle: [BUG] Query.Or is very slow
overshoot: Three things go beyond what #1644 needs. (1) `CompiledExpressionCache.Add` was converted from lock-free CAS to a single global `lock (_publish)` for every publication of every expression kind, not just AND/OR — the body is tiny, but all first-compile publications across all threads now serialize on one monitor. (2) Every AND/OR predicate delegate is now a closure over `Lazy<T>`, so each evaluation pays a `Lazy.Value` read plus one extra delegate hop — per document, for every filtered query, for all users, forever (LiteDB/Document/Expression/BsonExpression.DeferredCompilation.cs:20-25). (3) Failure timing changed: a `lambda.Compile()` failure on an AND/OR expression now surfaces at first execution rather than at `BsonExpression.Create`, and `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication` caches that exception permanently for that instance. Test-side: `Discarded_unexecuted_boolean_trees_are_not_rooted_by_the_cache` depends on `GC.Collect` + `WeakReference` timing, and `Deferred_boolean_compilation_publishes_only_after_execution` reflects on the private static `_compiledCache` field — both fragile and beyond the report's scope.
reporterNeed: Building a 100-term OR predicate with `Query.Or(query, Query.EQ("field", i.ToString()))` in a loop took 2503 ms on 5.0.7 versus 2 ms on 4.1.4. The reporter only wants to assemble a query object cheaply; they never execute it in the repro. A commenter diagnosed the cause as And/Or re-rendering the whole expression to text and re-parsing it.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1644 with the measured before/after for their exact snippet, and state plainly what remains: composition still concatenates and re-parses (holyping's diagnosis), so it is still O(n^2) and the one large compile now happens at first execution instead of during the loop. Then add a test that pins the reporter's shape — build 100 chained `Query.Or` and assert the cache holds no compiled entry for any intermediate (the mechanism test #5 already has, applied to a 100-term chain) — since nothing currently guards the reported scenario. Optionally open a follow-up issue for composing the expression tree directly in `Query.Compose` instead of text round-tripping.
whatChanged: `Compile` no longer calls `lambda.Compile()` eagerly for expressions of type And/Or; it wraps the lambda in a `Lazy<BsonExpressionScalarDelegate>` that compiles and publishes to the shared cache only on first invocation. In the reporter's loop each iteration's root (and every interior OR node reached by the recursive `Compile` walk over Left/Right) is therefore never compiled — only the ~101 leaf `field = "..."` equality nodes are, and those hit the source-keyed cache. The quadratic pile of LINQ `Expression.Compile()` calls that produced the 2503 ms is gone; what remains in the loop is tokenizing/parsing plus ~5000 cheap `Expression.Lambda` + `Lazy` allocations.

issueTitle: [SUGGESTION] Improve query optimization
reporterNeed: Two logically identical LINQ queries — Where(x => x.Id >= low && x.Id <= high) vs Where(x => x.Id <= high && x.Id >= low), both OrderByDescending(Id).Limit(10) over 50k rows — ran 2x apart in wall time because the optimizer always picked the first indexable term, giving INDEX SCAN(_id >= 24900) in one case and INDEX SCAN(_id <= 25100) in the other. He wanted predicate order to stop mattering; in follow-up comments (after lbnascimento measured a BETWEEN plan as much faster than either) he asked LiteDB to fuse `x >= low && x <= high` into a single BETWEEN range scan.
whatChanged: Adds QueryOptimization.PreferRangeStart + IndexRange.HasCloserStart: when two candidates have the same cost (IndexRange.GetCost is always 20) and the same index expression, the one whose seek point is closest to the output's starting end wins — _start for ascending, _end for descending, with an inclusive/exclusive tie-break. For the reporter's descending query both term orders now select `_id <= 25100`, so both produce the same plan and the same timing. The second bound stays a post-load document filter; no BETWEEN fusion. The commit also adds LiteDB/Utils/BsonNumberComparison.cs, which nothing references at this commit, plus a test file for BsonValue mixed-type numeric comparison that the parent commit already implemented.
gap: The BETWEEN fusion he asked for in the comments is not done — the second bound is still a filter evaluated after LoadDocument, so an unbounded (no-Limit) range query still loads every document from the chosen bound to the end of the index instead of the ~201 in the range. His filed benchmark uses Limit(10), so that is not blocking him, but the plan lbnascimento told him was the fastest is still unreachable except by writing `$._id between @0 and @1` by hand.
overshoot: HasCloserStart only optimizes the scan prefix and ignores where the scan terminates. IndexCost.CreateIndex builds `>= v` as IndexRange(v, MaxValue) and `<= v` as IndexRange(MinValue, v), and IndexRange.Execute runs to the natural end of the index. For ascending order — the default whenever OrderBy does not match the index expression — the lower bound now always wins, so previously bounded scans become full-tail scans: col.Find(x => x.Id <= 100 && x.Id >= 1) on 50k rows went from INDEX SCAN(_id <= 100) (100 nodes) to INDEX SCAN(_id >= 1) (50k nodes scanned, 50k documents loaded by QueryPipe, then filtered to 100). Same for `key BETWEEN 1 AND 5 AND key > 3`, where the unbounded `key > 3` is now preferred over the bounded BETWEEN. Reversed_range_terms_seek_from_the_output_start pins this by asserting the ascending plan contains "key >", and only exercises it through Limit(5) where the choice is harmless. Before the commit users could steer this by predicate order (the workaround this issue thread itself taught); that control is now gone and the regression is silent. Separately, LiteDB/Utils/BsonNumberComparison.cs is dead code — grep at 304ccad2f9 finds only its definition — duplicating IsDecimalConvertible/OutOfDecimalRangeSign already present in the parent commit, and Issue1706NumericBounds_Tests.cs tests that pre-existing behaviour rather than anything this commit changes.
suggestedAction: Narrow the tie-break: apply PreferRangeStart only when the query has a Limit or Offset (where prefix waste is what costs), or make it compare expected scan span rather than only the start point so a bounded range (BETWEEN, or the tighter single bound) is never replaced by one that runs to the end of the index. Better still, do what the reporter asked and fuse two compatible bounds on the same index into one IndexRange, keeping the independent multikey ANY case excluded as the existing comment notes. Drop BsonNumberComparison.cs and Issue1706NumericBounds_Tests.cs from this commit — they belong to the earlier mixed-type comparison change. Then reply on the issue: predicate order no longer changes the plan, but BETWEEN fusion is still open, so `$._id between @0 and @1` remains the fastest form for a bounded range without a limit.

issueTitle: [BUG] Query.And produce incorrect query.
reporterNeed: On 5.0.8, combining two LINQ-derived predicates via `Query.And(mapper.GetExpression<StateModel,bool>(x => x.A == 1), mapper.GetExpression<StateModel,bool>(x => x.B == 2))` and running `col.Query().Where(query).ToList()` returned 0 documents instead of 1. Each `GetExpression` call independently numbers its parameters from `@p0`, and the old `Query.And` only concatenated `left.Source + " AND " + right.Source` into a string, which the implicit `string -> BsonExpression` conversion re-parsed with an empty parameter document — so both `@p0` references were unbound (null) and nothing matched. No comments on the issue; single reporter, single problem.
whatChanged: `Query.And`/`Query.Or` now call a new `Query.Compose` (LiteDB/Client/Structures/Query.Composition.cs) instead of returning a string. It tokenizes each operand's `Source`, rewrites every `@word`/`@int` parameter reference to a fresh `@q<N>` name, copies the operand's bound values into one merged `BsonDocument`, and builds the result with `BsonExpression.Create("(left OP right)", parameters)`. The rewrite mirrors the parser exactly (`TryParseParameter` runs before `TryParsePath`, so `@word` is always a parameter; bare `@` current-item and `@.field` are left alone, and `@` inside string/quoted-field tokens is never touched). Because `@key` in GROUP BY HAVING would otherwise be renamed away, a new `internal HashSet<string> BsonExpression.GroupKeyAliases` records the renamed group-key slots and `GroupByPipe.SetKeyParameter` binds them alongside `"key"` per group. For the reporter: the query becomes `($.A = @q0 AND $.B = @q1)` with q0=1, q1=2, and returns the one expected document.
gap: None material. The first test is the reporter's code almost verbatim (same two-field model, same `GetExpression` pair, same `Query.And`) using `col.Find(query)` rather than `col.Query().Where(query)`; both funnel into the same predicate, so the reporter's exact call shape is covered in substance.
overshoot: Real but secondary: (1) Silent break of the natural workaround for this very bug. Composing expressions with *unbound* parameters and then binding them by name on the result — `var q = Query.And(BsonExpression.Create("$.A=@a"), BsonExpression.Create("$.B=@b")); q.Parameters["a"]=1;` — worked before (the composed expression kept the original `@a`/`@b` names). Compose deliberately renames unbound parameters too ("so another operand cannot bind them accidentally", pinned by `Unbound_parameters_remain_unbound_...`), so `q.Parameters["a"]=1` is now a silent no-op and the caller must know the undocumented `q0`/`q1` scheme. No exception, no diagnostic, just wrong results. Nothing in the issue asks for this. (2) `Query.And/Or` now tokenize and re-parse on every call; the variadic overloads fold left, so an n-way `And` re-tokenizes the accumulated source n times (O(n²) in source length). Previously it was string concatenation with one parse at the end. (3) The composed `.Source` text changes (parameter names rewritten), which anyone logging or re-feeding `.Source` into `db.Execute` will see. (4) Composition snapshots parameter *values* by reference, not deep copy, so the test's "composition snapshots parameter bindings" claim holds for scalars but not for a mutated `BsonDocument`/`BsonArray` parameter value — the assertion is slightly stronger than the implementation.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1715 confirming the fix with the concrete before/after (`@p0` collision plus dropped parameter document -> both sides unbound -> 0 rows; now renamed to `@q0`/`@q1` with values merged). Separately, add an XML-doc line on `Query.And`/`Query.Or` stating that the returned expression's parameters are renamed `q0..qN` and that setting values on the result by the operands' original names has no effect — otherwise the silent no-op in the overshoot note (1) will produce a new bug report.

gap: Nothing in the reporter's scenario. Two non-code gaps: (1) issue #1829 is still OPEN with the last maintainer word being "I'm honestly not sure what to do... one possibility is to document this limitation" — nobody has told toumir/AlBannaTechno that composed predicates now work, in which version, or that the same-named-nested-scope case lbnascimento worried about is preserved; (2) the new `NotSupportedException` boundary ("Invoked query arguments must be parameters, constants, or document member paths") is undocumented — a user who partially applies a captured value, e.g. `Expression.Invoke(lambda, root, Expression.Field(Expression.Constant(closure), "min"))`, gets that message with no hint that the fix is to inline the value as `Expression.Constant(value)`.
issueTitle: [QUESTION] Predicate Order matter ?
overshoot: Small and mostly defensible, but real: (1) a new `NotSupportedException` is thrown when an invoked lambda's argument is a method call or a member chain rooted at a constant (captured closure field) instead of a parameter/constant/parameter-rooted path. Under the old code those cases went through the `base.VisitInvocation` + `_builder.Length--` hack, which chopped one character off the translated argument and almost always ended in a BsonExpression parse failure anyway — so this trades a confusing error for a clearer one rather than breaking working code, but it is a hard-coded restriction the report never asked for, and two tests (`Volatile_invocation_arguments_are_rejected_instead_of_duplicated`, `Captured_field_arguments_are_not_silently_omitted`) pin `NotSupportedException` as required behaviour. (2) Closed invocations (no root parameter, no server runtime) are now evaluated client-side as a constant in `VisitInvocation` — a behaviour change beyond the report, pinned by `Invocation_inside_a_captured_index_keeps_single_client_evaluation` (exactly one getter read). (3) Every LINQ→BsonExpression translation now pays one extra `InvocationExpander` tree walk in the `LinqExpressionVisitor` constructor; cheap (it short-circuits on parameterless subtrees) but paid by all users. (4) `_expr` is now the rewritten tree, so the `NotSupportedException` messages from `Resolve` print the expanded expression rather than what the user wrote.
reporterNeed: toumir combined two separately-declared predicates with the Albahari `PredicateBuilder.Or` (`Expression.Invoke(expr2, expr1.Parameters)`) and got different results depending on operand order: `p2.Or(p1)` counted 2, `p1.Or(p2)` counted 0 with `p1 = p => false`, `p2 = p => p.Name.Contains("a")`. He said he was stuck for three weeks because his whole refactor was built on composed predicates. Root cause per lbnascimento: since v5.0.8 the visitor compares `ParameterExpression` identity, so the invoked lambda's parameter is treated as nested scope `@` instead of root `$`, and the right-hand operand silently matches nothing.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1829 (once PR #2917 lands) telling toumir and AlBannaTechno that PredicateBuilder-style `Or`/`And` composition now works in both operand orders because invocations of literal lambdas are inlined (parameters substituted) before scope analysis, that lbnascimento's `x => x.Names.Any(x => x.Length > 5)` same-name-nested-scope case is explicitly covered by a test, and name the version. Also state the one remaining restriction — arguments passed to an invoked lambda must be parameters, constants, or document member paths, otherwise `NotSupportedException`; bake captured values in with `Expression.Constant(value)`.
whatChanged: A new `InvocationExpander` runs over the whole expression in the `LinqExpressionVisitor` constructor before any scope analysis: every `InvocationExpression` whose target is a literal `LambdaExpression` is inlined by substituting the lambda's parameters with the invocation arguments (with alpha-renaming of nested binders so a free argument cannot be captured by an identically-named inner lambda). The old golden test that documented the bug (`(($._id>=@p0) AND (((@._id<=@p1))=true))`) is corrected to `(($._id>=@p0) AND ($._id<=@p1))` and now also asserts the composed expression agrees with the compiled delegate.

issueTitle: [BUG] Aggregate functions ignore pragma UTC_DATE
reporterNeed: pcjmuenster (LiteDB 5.0.8, .NET Framework 4.7.2) set the UTC_DATE pragma; loading a whole record gave DateTimeKind.Utc, but `GetCollection<Entry>().Max(e => e.Timestamp)` gave a DateTimeKind.Local value, so they had to wrap every aggregate result in DateTime.ToUniversalTime(). They wanted the pragma honored uniformly in query/aggregate expressions, not only in full-document reads. lbnascimento could not reproduce on 5.0.8/5.0.9; the report never says whether an index existed on Timestamp, which is the decisive detail.
whatChanged: `IndexLookup` (the covered-index "index-key-only" loader used by Min/Max/Select on an indexed field) no longer returns the raw index key when that key contains a DateTime; it loads the document from the data block instead and then applies the pragma (UTC kept as-is, or ToLocalTime when UTC_DATE is off, with DateTime.Min/MaxValue left as Unspecified sentinels). It also fixes a second, unrelated-to-dates defect in the same class: `Load(PageAddress rawId)` used to call `_indexer.GetNode(rawId)` on what is actually a data-block address (doc.RawId = node.DataBlock), so covered-index queries that go through sort replay or group/aggregate replay were reading an index node out of a data page. That path now goes through a DatafileLookup. Net effect for the reporter: `col.Max(x => x.Timestamp)` / `Min` return the same DateTime instant and the same Kind as `FindById`, for both pragma settings, indexed or not.
gap: The exact symptom direction in the report is still unexplained. On this codebase the pre-fix covered-index path returned the key with DateTimeKind.Utc *always* — i.e. it was wrong when UTC_DATE is off, and already correct when UTC_DATE is on, which is the opposite of "pragma on, got Local" and matches lbnascimento's non-repro. The commit enforces the invariant the reporter asked for, but if their 5.0.8 symptom had a different root cause it is not identified. One inverted decode survives: BufferReader.ReadDateTime is `_utcDate ? date.ToLocalTime() : date` (LiteDB/Engine/Disk/Serializer/BufferReader.cs:243) while the document decoder BsonElementReader.cs:91 is `utcDate ? date : date.ToLocalTime()`. That path only feeds sort-container keys (ordering), not returned values, so it does not leak into results — but it is the one place in the engine that turns a UTC date into Local when UTC_DATE is on, and the commit does not touch it.
overshoot: The covered-index optimization is abandoned for every date-bearing index key, unconditionally: `if (ContainsDate(node.Key)) return this.Load(node.DataBlock);` runs even when UtcDate is true, where the key was already the correct value. Index keys are written as `value.ToUniversalTime().Ticks` (BufferSliceExtensions.cs:294, unchanged since pre-5.0) and BsonValue truncates to millisecond precision in its constructor, so the key and the stored document agree to the millisecond — a ToLocalTime() on the key (or skipping the document load when UtcDate is true) would have been enough. As written, a query like `Query().Where("stamp > X").Select("stamp")` over a date index now performs one random data-block read per row where it previously read none; Min/Max pay one extra read (negligible), large covered scans pay a lot. Secondary: GetPlan still reports `loader: "index"` for these queries (QueryPlan.cs:171) although documents are now being read, and the tests assert that string, pinning the misleading label. The test `Covered_dates_match_document_decoding_during_a_repeated_local_hour` also pins exact tick-for-tick parity with document decoding, an expectation stricter than the report.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1851 that covered-index/aggregate reads now follow UTC_DATE and that the ToUniversalTime() workaround can be dropped, and state honestly that the reported direction (pragma on -> Local) could not be reproduced — in current code the covered path returned Utc unconditionally, so the bug bit hardest with UTC_DATE off; ask whether Timestamp was indexed in their app if they can still check. Separately, consider skipping the document load when pragmas.UtcDate is true (the key is already the correct UTC instant) to keep the covered-index fast path, and either relabel the plan loader or drop the `loader == "index"` assertions that now describe a document read.
