issueTitle: Collection.include(x => x.document).find(Query.all()... ) return null
overshoot: None material. The change is confined to `LiteCollection<T>.Find(Query, skip, limit)`: no new public API, no new exceptions, no changed defaults, no validation added. The execution-query copy now also triggers when `_includes.Count > 0` (previously only on paging), which costs one small `Query` allocation for callers who already opted into includes, and means a caller mutating their `Query` object after calling `Find` but before enumerating no longer sees that mutation on this path — the paging path already behaved that way. The only behaviour anyone could "lose" is refs staying unexpanded despite calling `.Include(...)`, which is the bug. The ordering expectation the tests pin (collection includes before query includes) is not arbitrary: it matches `collection.Query().Include(...)` and is required for nested paths like `$.First.Address` to resolve.
reporterNeed: On LiteDB v5 they called `collection.Include(x => x.document).Find(Query.All(), 0, 100)` and got the referenced document back with only `Id` populated and every other property null, while `.Include(...).FindAll()` returned it fully populated. They wanted the first form (paged, Query-based) to resolve DbRefs too.
suggestedAction: Comment on the issue: this was real — the `Find(Query, skip, limit)` overload never passed the collection-level `.Include(...)` list to the engine, so only the stored `$id`/`$ref` stub was mapped; fixed in PR #2917, and the documented workaround until a release is `query.Includes.Add("$.Document")` (as fubar-coder posted in 2020) or `collection.Query().Include(x => x.Document).Skip(0).Limit(100).ToEnumerable()`.
whatChanged: `LiteCollection<T>.Find(Query, skip, limit)` previously built its local execution query only when paging was requested, and in either branch copied only `query.Includes` — the collection's `_includes` (from `.Include(x => x.Document)`) were silently dropped, so DbRef stubs were never expanded. The commit makes the copy path trigger when `_includes.Count > 0` as well and does `executionQuery.Includes.AddRange(_includes)` before `AddRange(query.Includes)`. All other `Query` fields were already copied, so nothing is lost. Running the reporter's exact call now: `_includes` non-empty → includes reach the pipeline → `BasePipe.Include` resolves each `$id`/`$ref` → all properties populated. `FindOne(Query)` and `FindById` go through the same overload and are fixed as a side effect.

issueTitle: [BUG] Quering Based On Referenced Entity Failed After Creating The Index
reporterNeed: On LiteDB 5.0.9, `humans.Include(h => h.Homes).Query().Where(Query.Any().EQ("$.Homes[*].Value", 655555))` returned the right Humans until he ran `humans.EnsureIndex("$.Homes[*].Value")`; after that the same query returned nothing. He wanted correct results *and* an index he could lean on, because (his later comment) the two-step workaround "will degrade the performance to the worst level when using pagination". He also asked, unanswered, how to query a named index explicitly (`EnsureIndex("home_value", ...)` then `Query.GTE("home_value", 0)`), noting it does not work even for plain nested arrays.
whatChanged: Root cause: the Humans documents store `{$ref,$id}` stubs, so an index on `$.Homes[*].Value` only ever contains nulls; once it existed the planner picked it and the seek matched nothing, while INCLUDE resolved the real values only afterwards. The commit adds `QueryOptimization.Includes.cs` and filters the candidate index list in `ChooseIndex`: any ordinary index whose member path lies under an INCLUDE path (except the `$id` leaf, which the include preserves) is dropped. The reporter's query therefore falls back to the `_id` full scan, `DefineIncludes` puts the include in `IncludeBefore`, and the filter runs on resolved documents — correct results, index present or not. `BasePipe.DoInclude` additionally stops the referenced document from overwriting `$id` (and now matches `_id`/`$id` case-insensitively) so `$.ref.$id` indexes stay usable.
gap: The index he created is now silently a no-op: the planner skips it and full-scans `_id`, resolving every reference per document. Nothing tells him — no exception, no warning at `EnsureIndex`, and only `GetPlan()` reveals the fallback. So his actual goal (indexed, paginated queries over a `[BsonRef]` field) is still unreachable and he has no way to learn that from the library; he will keep creating indexes that do nothing. His second question (how to use a named index explicitly, including for plain nested arrays) is untouched by the commit.
overshoot: The exclusion is conservative by design: `IncludeChangesIndex` returns true (drop the index) whenever `TryGetMemberPath` cannot parse the expression, so indexes that are actually valid get dropped too — filtered-array paths (`$.refs[@.x=1].$id`), function- or arithmetic-wrapped paths (`LOWER($.ref.$id)`), and any index over `$`, which is now excluded for *every* query that carries any INCLUDE. Those users silently lose a working index plan (index seek → `_id` full scan) with no diagnostic. The same applies to ORDER BY: `Issue1904Planning_Tests` pins that an order-by on an included field no longer reuses the index and falls back to an explicit (possibly disk-backed) sort. The `BasePipe` change also broadens `_id` exclusion from exact to case-insensitive, i.e. a referenced document with an `_ID` field silently stops contributing it — beyond anything the report needs (a later commit in the same PR, #1920, reworks that line again). Planning tests also assert internal plan names, e.g. that a non-include query still uses `reference_value` and matches `$.ref.value = null` for 2 rows, pinning stale-stub indexing as guaranteed behaviour.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1904 with the honest answer: (1) his query returns correct results again with the index present — fixed in #2917, covered by `LiteDB.Tests/Issues/Issue1904_Tests.cs` using his exact `Human`/`Home` model; (2) an index on a `[BsonRef]` field can never accelerate anything, because the parent document only stores `{$ref,$id}` — the planner now skips such indexes instead of returning wrong results, so he should drop `EnsureIndex("$.Homes[*].Value")`; (3) for indexed pagination, either index `Value` on the `Homes` collection and drive the query from there via `$.Homes[*].$id ANY = ...` (which *is* still index-backed after this fix), or denormalize `Value` onto `Human`; (4) LiteDB 5 has no "query by index name" — you query by expression and the planner matches an index whose expression is textually identical, which is why `Query.GTE("home_value", 0)` never worked. Separately, consider a follow-up issue for surfacing the skip (warn or throw on `EnsureIndex` over a `BsonRef` path, or expose it in `GetPlan`), and for narrowing the conservative `TryGetMemberPath` fallback so function-wrapped and filtered-array indexes are not dropped wholesale.

gap: Nothing material for the reporter. Residual: the fix lives in PR #2917, still open/unreleased, and issue 1908 has had no maintainer reply since 2020 — the reporter has never been told the diagnosis (captured collections are bound as a whole BsonArray parameter `@p0`, and `@p0[0]` is not parseable BsonExpression).
issueTitle: [BUG] Cannot support Linq expression with array index
overshoot:
Real but secondary; three items.
1) New exception on a path that worked: a runtime-valued index into a row/captured collection, e.g. `x.Factors[DateTime.Now.Day]` or `x.Values[DateTime.Now.ToString()]`, previously client-folded to `$.Factors[18]`. `TryVisitCapturedElement` now throws NotSupportedException("Server runtime expressions cannot be evaluated as captured indexes.") — and `Issue1908_Tests.Runtime_positional_indexes_are_rejected_on_rows_and_captures` pins that as required behaviour. Neither #1908 nor #2367 asks for this; a fallback to the old client evaluation would be the conservative choice.
2) Semantics change for captured sequences beyond indexing: `IsElementAccess` also claims First/FirstOrDefault/Last/LastOrDefault/Single/SingleOrDefault/Min/Max. On a captured (non-row) sequence these used to translate server-side via EnumerableResolver (`MIN(@p0)`, `@p0[0]`, `@p0[-1]`) and are now folded with CLR semantics. On an empty captured collection that flips a null/MinValue result into a thrown InvalidOperationException. Only `get_Item`/ArrayIndex/ElementAt were needed for this report.
3) Stricter validation and a small cost everyone pays: `x.Values[""]` / `x[""]` now throws NotSupportedException("Empty row dictionary keys...") instead of emitting `$.['']`; `x.Factors.ElementAt(x.Id)` now throws where it used to emit `$.Factors[$._id]`; and `Resolve` runs `ValidateCapturedRuntimeBranches` plus per-node ElementAccessVisitor/ServerRuntimeVisitor sweeps on every LINQ translation. The dictionary-key JSON escaping (`JsonSerializer.Serialize(key, …)`) is unrelated to this report but is a genuine expression-injection fix (key `a'b] OR true` previously escaped the path).
reporterNeed: On LiteDB 5.0.9, `collection.Find(item => item["Factor"] == parameters[0])` with a captured local `string[] parameters` threw NotSupportedException — the translator emitted `($.['Factor'] = @p0[0])` and the parser failed with "Unexpected token `[` in position 19". The same query with a string literal worked. They just wanted to pass a value out of a captured array into a LINQ predicate.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1908: explain the cause (captured collections were emitted whole as `@p0` and the trailing `[0]` was not valid BsonExpression), state that captured element access — arrays, List, Dictionary, multidimensional, explicit IndexExpression — is now evaluated CLR-side into a parameter, and link PR #2917. Separately, reconsider throwing on `x.Factors[DateTime.Now.Day]`: restoring client evaluation there (and relaxing the test that pins the throw) removes the only behaviour regression this change introduces.
whatChanged: A new `TryVisitCapturedElement`/`TryVisitCapturedElementMember`/`TryVisitCapturedBranch`/`TryVisitCapturedUnary` layer intercepts element access whose source does not depend on the query row and folds the whole access to a CLR constant, which then becomes a normal `@p0` parameter. Traced on the reporter's expression: `item["Factor"]` still goes down the row path (its indexed source is the lambda parameter, so `TryVisitCapturedElement` returns false) and yields `$.['Factor']`; `parameters[0]` is an ArrayIndex over a captured constant with a non-row index, so it is evaluated to `"Base"` and emitted as `@p0`. Result `($.['Factor'] = @p0)` parses and runs. Expressions containing `DateTime.Now`/`UtcNow`/`Today`/`Guid.NewGuid` are deliberately kept on the server path.

issueTitle: [BUG] BsonRef Key field not set
reporterNeed: On LiteDB 5.0.10 / .NET 4.7.2, the reporter queried `col.Include(x => x.Corso).Include(x => x.Dipendente).Include(x => x.Dipendente.Cliente).Query().Where(...).Select(x => new { Articolo = x.Corso, Cliente = x.Dipendente.Cliente, ... })` and the projected referenced objects came back fully populated except `Id == 0`. The same query without `Select` was correct. They then re-saved those objects and wrote `{"$id":0,"$ref":"Articolo"}` into their database, i.e. silent data corruption. They wanted the Id populated (or an error), not a "call ToArray() first" workaround.
whatChanged: In `LiteDB/Engine/Query/Pipeline/BasePipe.cs` `DoInclude`, the merge of the resolved reference document into the ref stub no longer skips `_id` (it still skips `$id`, so both keys are now present), and it promotes the stub's `$type` to `_type`. Previously the `$id`→`_id` promotion only happened inside `RegisterDbRefItem`/`RegisterDbRefList`'s custom member deserializer, which is bypassed when the resolved sub-document is projected standalone into an anonymous type — hence Id == 0. Keeping `$id` preserves the LINQ translation of `x.Ref.Id` to `$.Ref.$id` (LinqExpressionVisitor.cs:632). Include runs before Select in QueryPipe, so the projection now sees `_id`.
gap: Two leftovers, neither blocking the reporter's own query. (1) If a user projects a DbRef member *without* `.Include()`, the stub `{$id, $ref}` is still deserialized into a plain anonymous-type member as an all-default object with Id == 0 — the same silent wrong result, with no exception and no test; mbdavid explicitly asked for "works or throw an informative exception". (2) Rows the reporter already corrupted with `{"$id":0,"$ref":"..."}` are not detected or repaired; nothing tells them which rows are affected. The second commenter (HofmeisterAn, manual `BsonMapper.Global.Deserialize<List<IItem>>(items)` inside a readonly struct constructor) is very likely fixed by the same `_id`/`_type` promotion, but no test covers that path.
overshoot: Small but real. (a) Every included sub-document now carries a duplicated `_id` next to `$id` for all users, including raw `db.GetCollection("x").Include("$.Ref")` consumers who serialize or re-save documents; `Issue1920Projection_Tests.Nested_and_array_projections_keep_custom_ids_without_changing_stubs` pins that exact new shape (`raw["_id"]==23 && raw["$id"]==23 && !ContainsKey("$ref")`) as contract. (b) The `$type`→`_type` promotion addresses polymorphic DbRef, which the report never mentions; when a stub's recorded `$type` disagrees with the stored document's own `_type`, the stale stub now wins in projections (consistent with the pre-existing precedence in BsonMapper.cs:292-295, so not a regression, but it is unrequested scope). (c) The same test asserts `db.GetCollection("items").FindById(7).ContainsKey("_type") == false`, pinning unrelated mapper discriminator behaviour that nothing in the report justifies.
suggestedAction: Comment on #1920 confirming the fix with a repro-shaped snippet, and add the one caveat the reporter needs: the Id is only populated when the reference is actually `Include`d — projecting a DbRef member without `Include` still yields a default-valued object with Id 0. Optionally open a small follow-up issue for that non-included projection case (return null or throw rather than a silent zero Id), since it is the same failure mode mbdavid asked to be made explicit.

gap: The fix is silent about its cost. For the reporter's own prefix ("さ", any non-ASCII-alphanumeric prefix) the query now takes the FULL INDEX SCAN path (GetCost 100) instead of a seek — correct results, but the index they deliberately created no longer accelerates the query, and nothing tells them so except running EXPLAIN. They are also never told the workaround that would restore a seek for Japanese prefixes (open the DB with an Ordinal collation, e.g. `collation=ja-JP/Ordinal` or `Collation.Binary`, at which point `_usePrefixSeek` is taken). Additionally, on netstandard2.0 consumers running .NET Framework (or .NET with NLS mode), `LikePrefixRange.IsSupported` is false, so even plain ASCII `LIKE 'Mau%'` loses the seek under the default collation — a regression those users get with no diagnostic.
issueTitle: [BUG] Wrong 'StartsWith' result when EnsureIndex() to non-ascii string column
overshoot: Three things go beyond the report. (1) Indexed LIKE now follows the collation instead of the hardcoded OrdinalIgnoreCase prefix/equality test. The commit's own edit to `LiteDB.Tests/Engine/Index_Tests.cs` pins the consequence: under `tr-TR/IgnoreCase`, `name LIKE 'maUriCIO'` goes from 4 matches to 0. That is arguably right (it now agrees with the unindexed path), but it is a visible behaviour change for Turkish-style collations that nobody reported. (2) `_testSqlLike |= collation.SortOptions == CompareOptions.OrdinalIgnoreCase` forces an extra `SqlLike` call per candidate for every OrdinalIgnoreCase database, and `LiteDB.Tests/Query/LikeCollation_Tests.cs` pins the expectation that supplementary case pairs (U+10400 vs U+10428) do NOT fold under OrdinalIgnoreCase — an expectation the report does not justify, and one a user could equally call a bug. (3) Query-plan cost: `LikePrefixRange.TryGetUpperBound` probes the collation ~174 times per prefix (62 ASCII alphanumerics + 0x70 combining marks), plus `IsCaseStable` and a 62-entry sort per character in `GetSuccessor`, on every culture-collation LIKE query construction — paid by every user, including the ASCII ones who had no problem.
reporterNeed: On LiteDB 5.0.11 / .NET 6 / Windows with the default collation (CurrentCulture/IgnoreCase), the reporter stored 1000 rows of random hiragana strings and ran `col.Find(x => x.Name.StartsWith("さ"))`. Without `EnsureIndex(x => x.Name)` the result count was right; with the index it silently returned fewer rows than actually existed. He needs an indexed StartsWith/LIKE prefix query on non-ASCII (\u30xx) text to return the same set as the unindexed one — silently losing rows is the whole complaint. Single-reporter issue, zero comments, still open.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2144 with the honest answer, then close on merge: "Fixed in #2917. Root cause: the index is ordered by your culture collation, but the prefix scan compared with OrdinalIgnoreCase and stopped at the first non-matching key — under a linguistic sort, keys starting with さ are interleaved with keys that do not, so the scan exited early. LIKE now only takes the seek path when a collation-safe key range can be proven (ordinal collations, or ASCII letter/digit prefixes under ICU); a non-ASCII prefix like さ falls back to a full index scan, so the result is now correct but the Name index no longer speeds that query up. If you need a seek on Japanese prefixes, open the database with an ordinal collation (`collation=ja-JP/Ordinal`), which restores the fast path with byte-order semantics." Worth also noting in the PR/release notes that on .NET Framework / NLS mode even ASCII prefix LIKE now full-scans, since that is the cost other users pay.
whatChanged: `IndexLike` now takes the `Collation` (plumbed from `IndexCost.CreateIndex`) and picks its execution path from it: the old OrdinalIgnoreCase prefix seek (`ExecuteStartsWith`) is used only for Ordinal/OrdinalIgnoreCase collations; for a culture collation a new `LikePrefixRange.TryGetUpperBound` tries to prove a safe `[prefix, upper)` key range (only for ASCII letter/digit prefixes, only under ICU, only after probing case variants and 174 followers for contractions) and uses `ExecuteRange`, where `SqlLike` with the collation still decides each key; otherwise it degrades to `ExecuteLike`, a full index scan with a per-key collation-aware `SqlLike`. For the reporter's default CurrentCulture/IgnoreCase collation and the prefix "さ", `isOrdinal` is false and `TryGetUpperBound` rejects the non-ASCII prefix, so the query takes the full index scan and returns exactly the unindexed result set. `GetCost`/`ToString` were updated to report 100 / "FULL INDEX SCAN" for that case. `LiteDB.Tests/Issues/Issue2144_Tests.cs` reproduces the reporter's scenario almost literally (hiragana U+3042..U+3092 rows, `col.Find(x => x.Name.StartsWith("さ"))` asserted equal to a `CompareInfo.IsPrefix` baseline, before indexing, after `EnsureIndex`, and after reopening the file) under both en-US and ja-JP IgnoreCase.

issueTitle: Inherited private Id setter is missed during deserialization with a parameterless constructor
overshoot:
Two items, both small and defensible, neither asked for by the report:
1) `Reflection.Expression.cs` recovers the invisible setter for EVERY inherited property, not just `_id`: any base-class property with a `private set` (or `internal set` from another assembly) now gets written on deserialization where it was silently skipped before. It aligns inherited behaviour with same-class private setters (which LiteDB already writes), but it is a silent semantic change for anyone who relied on an inherited private-setter property keeping its constructor/initializer value after a load. Not gated by `IncludeNonPublic`.
2) `Insert.cs` adds a new `LiteException(PROPERTY_READ_WRITE)` on a path the report never hits (genuinely read-only id, e.g. the test's `HiddenReadOnlyRow`). Previously that path inserted the document and then threw `NullReferenceException` from `_id.Setter(...)`; now it throws before `_engine.Insert`, so nothing is persisted (the test pins `Count() == 0`). Strictly an improvement over an NRE, but it is a behaviour change — a caller that swallowed the NRE used to end up with the row in the database — and it is pre-existing cleanup bundled into this fix rather than something #2225 needs.
reporterNeed: They have `class SomeClass : Base<Guid>` where `Id` is declared in the generic base as `public T Id { get; private set; }` and set via `SetId()`, plus `Value` and `List<SomeClass> Children`, and want `FindAll()` to give them back objects with `Id` populated. With only the `(Guid id, int value)` constructor they reported `INVALID_CTOR` ("Failed to create instance…"); adding a parameterless constructor made it load, but `Id` came back `Guid.Empty`.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2225 closing the loop honestly: (a) the reproducible half — inherited private `Id` setter staying `Guid.Empty` with a parameterless ctor — is fixed in v6 by re-resolving the property from its declaring type; (b) the originally reported `INVALID_CTOR` was never reproducible from the posted snippet and is not what this commit changes: state the actual ctor rule so they can self-diagnose — LiteDB picks a parameterized ctor only when EVERY parameter matches a mapped member by name (case-insensitive) and by exact type, a parameterless ctor always wins unless `[BsonCtor]` marks another, and `Children`-style members simply must not be ctor parameters unless a member of that exact type/name exists. Optionally file a follow-up to make the INVALID_CTOR message name the parameter that failed to bind, since that is the diagnostic the reporter actually lacked.
whatChanged: `Reflection.CreateGenericSetter` now detects the case where a property reached through a derived type reports `CanWrite == false` only because reflection hides a base class's private setter (`ReflectedType != DeclaringType`), re-fetches the `PropertyInfo` from the declaring type with `NonPublic | DeclaredOnly`, and builds a working setter from it. So `Base<Guid>.Id { get; private set; }` is now populated on deserialization of `SomeClass`, and the auto-id write-back after `Insert` also works. A derived type that hides the member with its own read-only property (`new Guid Id => …`) is left alone, and for that genuinely read-only case `RemoveDocId` now throws `LiteException(PROPERTY_READ_WRITE)` with a message instead of the previous `NullReferenceException` from `_id.Setter`. Two xunit tests: `Row` (base private setter + parameterless ctor + parameterized ctor: insert, FindAll, Id and Value preserved, Update round-trip, no duplicate rows) and `IntegerRow`/`HiddenReadOnlyRow` (auto-id write-back across a reopen; read-only id throws and inserts nothing).

gap: Suppression is conditional on a round-trip check (member has a readable getter and `Equals(getter(instance), ctorArg)`), which nobody documents. No docs/changelog entry in the commit.
issueTitle: [BUG] POCO with [BsonCtor] has its properties set twice (constructor + DeserializeObject)
overshoot: Three things go beyond the report, none fatal: (1) constructor arguments are now deserialised through `member.Deserialize` (MappedConstructor.Create -> DeserializeMember) instead of the old plain `this.Deserialize(paramType, doc[key])`, so custom member deserializers and [BsonRef] resolution now apply to ctor parameters — a real behaviour change for users who never hit #2303 (a later commit in the same PR adds the `isStored` guard so absent fields don't hit a decoder with Null). (2) Runtime cost paid by every parameterized-ctor type on every deserialize: two `AsyncLocal.Value` writes (ExecutionContext copy) per object, a ConditionalWeakTable add+remove, and an O(params) `Array.IndexOf` plus a getter invocation per member — on bulk `FindAll` of ctor-mapped entities this is per-document overhead that did not exist before. Parameterless types are exempted only from the second deserialize onward (first one still allocates a scope, since `entity.CreateInstance` is null until `CreateMappedInstance` assigns it). (3) The suppression is global and silent with no opt-out: any user whose ctor-bound setter has side effects it wanted on load (dirty flags, change notification, validation) loses them. No new public API, no new exception paths, no changed defaults beyond this.
reporterNeed: Reporter (LiteDB 5.0.15, .NET 7) has a POCO `Point` with a `[BsonCtor]` (double x, double y, double z) writing into a private `double[] _position`, and X/Y/Z properties backed by that array. On `FindAll()` LiteDB called the constructor with the stored values and then called X/Y/Z setters with the same values again, re-running the setters' side effects. He wants a parameterized constructor to be the only thing that populates the members it already received. No other commenters; no second problem under the issue.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2303 when the PR lands: confirm the double-population is gone for faithful constructors, and state the one condition explicitly — the setter is skipped only when the member has a readable getter that returns the value the constructor received, so a constructor that transforms or ignores its argument still gets its setter called afterwards (by design, so unbound and transformed members are not lost).
whatChanged: A parameterized constructor now runs inside a `ConstructorScope`: `MappedConstructor.Create` records (instance, source document, MemberMapper[], deserialised args) in a ConditionalWeakTable, and `DeserializeObject` skips the setter for any member that was a constructor parameter of that same document whose getter already returns the argument value (`HoldsValue`). Members not bound to a parameter, transformed/ignored arguments, getter-less or throwing members, and user-supplied `Ctor`/`_typeInstantiator` factories keep the old setter path. Running the reporter's program on this code prints only "Point Constructor x=1, y=2, z=3" on restore — X/Y/Z setters are not invoked, since each getter reads back exactly the double the constructor stored. `Issue2303_Tests.Constructor_bound_properties_are_not_set_again_but_unbound_properties_are` is his scenario (a [BsonCtor] Point with double coordinates and counting setters, plus an unbound Label that still gets set).

gap: Two residual items, neither caused by the commit. (1) The reporter's first attempt `t.MyEnumField == someEnum` still does not compile — that is a C# restriction on `==` for a type parameter constrained to `Enum`, not something LiteDB can fix; nothing in the repo or docs tells them `.Equals()` is the supported form, so they learn it only from this issue. Also, a type mismatch such as `x.Kind.Equals(0)` now returns zero rows silently rather than an error, so a user who mistypes the operand gets no diagnostic.
issueTitle: [BUG] generic Enums cannot be tested for equality in linq queries
overshoot: Minor and contained. The interception in VisitMethodCall fires only for 1-arg `Equals` declared on `Enum`/`object`/`ValueType` AND only when the unwrapped left operand is an enum, so `string.Equals`, other struct `ValueType.Equals`, and the existing ordinal-string path fall through unchanged; every shape it now handles previously threw NotSupportedException, so no working path changed. No new public API, no changed default, no measurable cost. One judgement call beyond the report: type-mismatched comparisons (`x.Kind.Equals(0)`, `.Equals("A")`, `.Equals(OtherEnum.A)`, `.Equals(null)`, and parameter-dependent cross-enum `x.Kind.Equals(x.Foreign)`) are folded to a constant `false` and silently match nothing. That is faithful to CLR `Enum.Equals(object)` and the tests pin it, but it is inconsistent with the sibling commit in the same PR (LinqExpressionVisitor.EnumOperands.cs), which throws an explanatory NotSupportedException for the analogous enum-vs-number mismatch.
reporterNeed: Reporter has a model implementing `MyInterface<K> where K : Enum` and wants to query it from a generic method `GetFoo<T,K>(K someEnum)`. `t.MyEnumField == someEnum` does not compile (C# forbids `==` on a type parameter), and the legal alternative `t.MyEnumField.Equals(someEnum)` threw `NotSupportedException: Method Equals not available to convert to BsonExpression`, leaving them with an ugly `(int)(object)` cast workaround that only holds when enums are stored as integers.
suggestedAction: When PR #2917 lands, close #2322 with a short note to the reporter: `.Equals()` on an enum member is now translated (including through a generic `K : Enum` and an interface-typed member access, in both EnumAsInteger modes), so the `(int)(object)` workaround can be dropped; `==` still will not compile because that is a C# restriction on type parameters, and `.Equals()` is the supported form. Optionally worth a follow-up issue on the silent-false vs. throw inconsistency between LinqExpressionVisitor.Enum.cs and LinqExpressionVisitor.EnumOperands.cs for enum/number mismatches.
whatChanged: Adds LinqExpressionVisitor.Enum.cs::TryVisitEnumEquals, called second in VisitMethodCall. For a 1-arg `Equals` declared on Enum/object/ValueType where the node depends on the lambda parameter, it strips boxing converts (to object/Enum/ValueType) from both operands; if the left is enum-typed and the right is a constant/closure that evaluates to the same enum type, it re-emits the call as `Expression.Equal(left, right)` with the value re-typed to the enum, which the normal binary path serializes through the mapper (correct under both EnumAsInteger settings). Running the reporter's tree `Convert(x, ITimeSeriesModel`1).Kind.Equals(Convert(closure.kind, Object))` through it yields `$.Kind = @p0`, so their query now works instead of throwing. Mismatched right operands (null, different type, different enum) fold to a constant `false`, which Resolve(predicate:true) wraps as `(@p0 = true)` and matches nothing rather than crashing.

gap: Only the same-member case is made atomic. When the ID is moved to a *different* member (oldId != p), the two writes are still unsynchronized: there is a window in which no member has FieldName "_id", so a concurrent ToDocument produces a document with no _id (and EntityMapper.Id is null). The issue title claims the method is not thread safe in general; a reporter who later repoints the ID at another property hits an unchanged race and gets no diagnostic. More broadly, EntityBuilder still mutates EntityMapper.Members with no lock (Ignore removes from the List while serialization enumerates it), so "configure the mapper only before use" remains an undocumented requirement.
issueTitle: [BUG] EntityBuilder<T>.Id method is not thread safe
overshoot: Production change is 1 condition (plus a BOM strip); nothing new is exposed, no default or API changes, no per-operation cost. Test-side only: Issue2324_Tests test 1 pins a mechanism rather than behaviour ("ResolveFieldName must never run for the existing ID") — a correct save/restore implementation would fail it; and test 3 is a 2x50,000-iteration barrier-synchronized stress test that adds real CI wall time for a race that test 1 already pins deterministically. Test 2 asserts pre-existing switch-the-ID behaviour the report did not ask about, but it does not change it.
reporterNeed: ltetak (LiteDB 5.x, incl. 5.0.15) reconfigures mapping at runtime on a live database: `BsonMapper.Global.Entity<T>().Id(idSelector)` while other threads are reading/writing. EntityBuilder.Id first reset the current _id member's FieldName back to ResolveFieldName(MemberName) and AutoId=false, then set it to "_id" again — and, as he explicitly diagnosed, in his case the old _id member and the newly selected member are the *same MemberMapper instance*, so for a moment the ID serialized as an ordinary field ("Key") instead of "_id". He wants v4's behaviour back, where reapplying the ID never went through a broken intermediate state.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2324: confirm the same-instance case he identified is now a no-op (ReferenceEquals guard), and state honestly that moving the ID to a *different* property is still not atomic and mapper configuration is still expected to happen before concurrent use — so he knows the guarantee he now has is "reapplying the same ID is safe", not "Id() is thread safe". If a general guarantee is wanted, open a follow-up for locking EntityMapper.Members mutations.
whatChanged: EntityBuilder.Id now skips the "reset the previous _id member" block when the previous _id member is the same object as the member being applied (`!ReferenceEquals(oldId, p)`). EntityMapper.GetMember returns the stored MemberMapper instance, so the reporter's repeated `Id(x => x.Key)` now leaves FieldName at "_id" throughout; the only remaining writes are `p.FieldName = "_id"` (same interned string) and `p.AutoId = autoId` (atomic bool). His window where the ID surfaced as an ordinary field is gone, and ResolveFieldName is no longer re-invoked for it.

issueTitle: [BUG] Cannot insert duplicate key in unique index '_id'. The duplicate value is '{"$date":"2006-04-02T07:00:00.0000000Z"}'.
reporterNeed: dwooten70 (5.0.17, .NET FW 4.8, Windows, US Eastern) uses an hourly `DateTime` as `_id` and bulk-inserts 480 rows from 2006-03-23 to 2006-04-11. His DateTimes are `Unspecified`, so LiteDB's `ToUniversalTime()` maps the nonexistent 2006-04-02 02:00 local onto the same instant as the real 03:00 EDT (both 07:00Z), and `InsertBulk` dies with a duplicate-key error for a value he can see is not duplicated in his data. His follow-up comment says the real complaint is broader: "LiteDB seems to automatically be shifting my times... I have even tried UTC and local but none of these resolved the issue. I see no way to prevent this." He fell back to storing `long` ticks, which costs him LiteDB Studio readability.
whatChanged: Two things. (1) Always on: `LiteException.IndexDuplicateKey` now appends a three-sentence hint to the message whenever the duplicated key is a DateTime whose `Kind != Utc` — explaining that DateTimes are stored as UTC, that the spring gap hour maps onto the following hour and the autumn hour repeats, and suggesting UTC keys or the new switch. (2) Opt-in, default off: `EngineSettings.RejectInvalidLocalTime` / `ConnectionString.RejectInvalidLocalTime` / connection-string key `reject invalid local time`. When on, Insert/Update/Upsert walk the document recursively before writing and throw `ArgumentException` if any Local/Unspecified DateTime satisfies `TimeZoneInfo.Local.IsInvalidTime`. Serializers, index keys, queries and JSON are untouched; the storage behaviour the reporter hit is unchanged by design.
gap:
His code on his data still throws exactly as before; only the message is longer. That is defensible (the collision is real), but the advice is incomplete in the one way he already flagged. The hint says "Use UTC values for keys" — he wrote that he "even tried UTC" and it did not help, because the `UtcDate` pragma defaults to false, so UTC-kind values come back Local-shifted on read. Neither the hint nor the new `docs/connection-string-parsing.md` section mentions `UtcDate`, yet the commit's own passing test needs `reopened.UtcDate = true` to make the round trip hold. So he follows the new advice and lands on the same wall.
No test covers his actual run: `Issue2357_Tests.Distinct_UTC_hour_ids...` is 480 hourly ids but `Kind=Utc` (the remedy, not his code); `Local_hour_ids_crossing_the_DST_gap...` uses his data shape but only with the opt-in flag on, asserting a different exception; the hint tests insert a genuinely duplicated 03:30 value rather than reproducing the gap collision. Nothing asserts "default settings + hourly Unspecified ids across the gap → duplicate-key error carrying the hint", which is the only thing he will actually see.
If he does enable the switch, the `ArgumentException` names neither the field nor the offending value (`paramName` is the literal "value"), so in a 480-document `InsertBulk` he still has to find the bad row himself.
overshoot:
The duplicate-key hint is unconditional on `Kind != Utc`, so every user who genuinely inserts the same local DateTime twice — the ordinary cause of this error — now gets a paragraph about daylight saving that does not apply, plus a pointer to a switch that will not help them. `Issue2357DuplicateKeyHint_Tests.Duplicate_local_DateTime_key_explains_how_two_local_times_become_one_key` pins precisely that: it inserts the identical value twice and asserts the DST lecture appears. Narrowing it with `IsInvalidTime`/`IsAmbiguousTime` on the incoming key would cost nothing. It is also a silent change to a public error message that existing user assertions may match on.
Beyond that, the report asked for his dates not to be shifted; it did not ask for a knob. The commit adds public surface on both `EngineSettings` and `ConnectionString` plus a parsed connection-string key, for a feature whose own XML doc concedes it "never fires on a UTC host" and "in zones that switch at midnight a date-only value can be rejected" — i.e. it can reject legitimate `DateTime.Date` values in e.g. America/Santiago. The thrown type is `ArgumentException`, outside LiteDB's `LiteException`/error-code model, so callers with `catch (LiteException)` will not catch it. All of this is opt-in and correctly defaulted off, so it is a design smell rather than a regression — not enough on its own for an OVERSHOOT verdict.
suggestedAction: Two small edits, then answer the reporter. (1) Gate the duplicate-key hint on the key actually being invalid or ambiguous in `TimeZoneInfo.Local`, so plain duplicates keep the plain message. (2) Add `UtcDate` to the hint and to the docs section — "store `DateTimeKind.Utc` values and set `db.UtcDate = true` (or pragma UTC_DATE) to read them back unshifted" — since that is the half of the remedy he reported as missing, and include the offending field path and value in the `ArgumentException` so bulk inserts are diagnosable. (3) Add one test at default settings: hourly Unspecified ids across the gap, assert the duplicate-key error and that it carries the hint. Then comment on #2357: the duplicate is genuine (02:00 and 03:00 EDT on 2006-04-02 are the same instant, 07:00Z), his ticks workaround is no longer needed — store Kind=Utc and set `UtcDate = true`, which keeps LiteDB Studio readable — and the opt-in switch exists if he wants the write rejected up front instead.

issueTitle: LINQ captured collection element members throw TargetException with non-null values
reporterNeed: lucaswhob had a class `MyVideoTbl` with a `DateTime Datetimepublish` property; inserting and querying every other column worked, but any query filtering on `Datetimepublish` threw `System.Reflection.TargetException`. He wants to filter a collection by that date. His three screenshots (class, query, stack trace) are dead mediafire links, so his exact query text, comparison value and LiteDB version are unrecoverable; the maintainer reconstructed the likely cause as comparing against a member of an element taken from a captured list (`x.Datetimepublish > videos[0].Datetimepublish`).
whatChanged: Adds LinqExpressionVisitor.CapturedMember.cs: when a non-row-dependent subtree contains an element access (indexer/get_Item, ArrayIndex, IndexExpression, First/Last/Single/ElementAt(+OrDefault), Min/Max), the whole subtree is compiled and evaluated in CLR and emitted as a single `@pN` parameter, instead of walking the legacy `_memberAccessNodes` stack which applied the member getter to the collection rather than the element (that mismatch is the TargetException). Covers indexers, dictionaries, arrays, multidimensional arrays, conditional/coalesce branches and implicit conversions, keeps short-circuit evaluation (unchosen branch never read), and keeps `DateTime.Now`/`Guid.NewGuid` server-side by throwing NotSupportedException where the two combine. Also folded in: dictionary keys are now JSON-escaped in the BSON path and an empty row dictionary key throws.
gap: The other cause the maintainer himself named in his first comment — a captured object that is null, e.g. `x.Datetimepublish > filter.From` with `filter == null`, which throws the same `TargetException` ("Non-static method requires a target") — is untouched. `TryVisitCapturedElementMember` only fires when `ElementAccessVisitor.Found`; a plain member chain over a null capture has no element access, falls through to the old `_memberAccessNodes` + `PropertyInfo.GetValue(null)` path and throws exactly as before, with the same message that tells the user nothing. Since the reporter's screenshots are gone, that variant is as consistent with his report as the collection one (arguably more so: he said only the date column failed). No commit in the branch addresses it. So: if his code was the list/dictionary shape he is unblocked and a test covers it; if it was a null captured filter object he is exactly where he was in 2023.
overshoot: `ValidateCapturedRuntimeBranches` + `ElementAccessVisitor.CheckBranch` compute `ContainsServerRuntime` over the *whole* binary/conditional node, not over the branch being checked. So any query tree containing `DateTime.Now/UtcNow/Today` or `Guid.NewGuid()` anywhere, plus a closed element access in the right operand of `&&`/`||`/`??`/`?:`, now throws NotSupportedException("Captured short-circuit branches combined with server runtime expressions are not supported."). Some of those shapes worked before: `Max()/Min()/First()` on a captured enumerable used to translate server-side (`MAX(@p0)`), so `x => x.Created < DateTime.Now && x.Id > ids.Max()` previously worked and now throws, while the same predicate with the clauses swapped still works — order-dependent failure with an opaque message. Additionally, `Min`/`Max` over captured collections switch from BSON comparison to CLR `IComparable` semantics, and the JSON-escaped dictionary keys / empty-key NotSupportedException are unrelated behaviour changes bundled into this commit. Translation-time cost also rises (an `ElementAccessVisitor` and one or more `ServerRuntimeVisitor` walks per member/method node, so ~O(n^2) on deep predicates) — parse time only, not query execution.
suggestedAction: Before closing #2367, comment with (1) the shape that is fixed and the version it ships in, and (2) an explicit statement that the null-captured-object variant he listed in his own first comment still throws `TargetException: Non-static method requires a target` — either open a follow-up for it or say it is by design (CLR would NRE) and keep the "read the value into a local first" workaround in the answer. Separately, narrow `CheckBranch` to test `ContainsServerRuntime` on the branch rather than the whole node, so `x => x.Created < DateTime.Now && x.Id > ids.Max()` does not regress from working to NotSupportedException depending on clause order.

gap: When constructor-parameter binding still fails (e.g. the parameter type does not exactly equal the member's DataType), LiteDB remains silent: the `[BsonCtor]` constructor is quietly skipped and the object is materialised another way, with no exception or warning. So a user in a near-miss variant of this scenario still has to guess. Also, the reporter is on 5.0.21 and PR #2917 is still open, so nothing is shipped to them yet.
issueTitle: [BUG] BsonCtor not called
overshoot:
Two changes go past the report, both modest:
1. `Activator.CreateInstance(type, args)` → `ctor.Invoke(args)`. The reporter never reached this line (their ctor was rejected during mapping), so this fixes an adjacent defect. It changes behaviour for anyone whose runtime argument types made Activator resolve to a *different* overload than the one the mapper selected — that path is pinned by the `SelectedOverload` test, an expectation the report does not justify (it is justified by `[BsonCtor]` semantics, though).
2. The FieldName fallback can make a previously-unmappable constructor mappable. For types with no parameterless constructor and several constructors, `Mappings.FirstOrDefault()` may now pick a different constructor than before, for users who did not ask. No new public API, no new exception, no perf cost (mapping is cached per type).
reporterNeed: After upgrading 5.0.17 → 5.0.21 their `[BsonCtor] PlayList(Guid _id, string name)` stopped being called, so the get-only `PlayListId`/`Id` came back as Guid.Empty and `col.FindById(pl.Id)` returned null for every document returned by `FindAll()`. They need the attributed constructor to receive the stored `_id` for a get-only Id that is an override of an abstract base property.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2578 once #2917 merges: the cause was that the `Id` member is mapped under the stored field name `_id` while the matcher only compared against the C# member name (`Id`), so the `_id` parameter never bound and the `[BsonCtor]` constructor was silently discarded; parameters now also match the stored field name. Name the release it lands in, and mention that a constructor parameter must still have exactly the member's CLR type or it is silently skipped.
whatChanged: In `GetTypeCtor` (LiteDB/Client/Mapper/BsonMapper.GetEntityMapper.cs), parameter→member matching gained a second pass: after matching on `MemberName` (now OrdinalIgnoreCase instead of `ToLower()`), it falls back to matching on `FieldName`. The reporter's `Id` property is the id member, so its FieldName is `_id` while its MemberName is `Id`; the old code compared only MemberName, found nothing for parameter `_id`, broke out of the loop and discarded the `[BsonCtor]` constructor entirely. With the fallback it binds to `_id`, both parameters resolve, and the attributed constructor is returned and invoked with the stored Guid. The commit also replaces `Activator.CreateInstance(type, args)` with `ctor.Invoke(args)` so the exact selected constructor runs rather than one re-resolved from runtime argument types.

issueTitle: [BUG] "Order By <computed_colum>" in SQL query doesn't have effect.
reporterNeed: MauMau666 (5.0.15 Studio / 5.0.21) ran `SELECT importo, importo + 20 as plus20 FROM fattura ORDER BY plus20 asc|desc` and got unsorted results, while `ORDER BY importo` sorted fine. They want ORDER BY on a SELECT alias for a computed column to sort by that computed value, like ORDER BY on a stored field does. No comments on the issue; no second problem reported under it.
whatChanged: `ParseSelectDocumentBuilder` now records explicitly-aliased projections (`SelectAliases`) and `Select.cs` resolves a bare Word in ORDER BY against that list (`ResolveSelectAlias` in the new `SelectAliases.cs`), replacing the `$.plus20` source path with the alias's own expression. Computed aliases get `RequiresExactSort = true`, which makes `QueryOptimization` skip the index-order shortcut and sort explicitly, and get recompiled via the new `BsonExpression.ExactCompilation.cs` so the Source-keyed delegate cache cannot hand back a delegate built from a differently-rounded literal. Volatile aliases (GUID() etc.) and GROUP BY / `UseSource` projections are deliberately excluded. Tracing the reporter's query: alias `plus20` matches, expression `importo + 20` becomes the sort key, both ASC and DESC sort correctly.
gap: Nothing for the reporter. Two adjacent shapes still silently do not resolve aliases and still sort by a non-existent source field: a projection whose fields set `UseSource` (e.g. `SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM c ORDER BY total` without GROUP BY) is skipped by the `!query.Select.UseSource` guard, and there is no error or hint when a bare ORDER BY word matches neither an alias nor a source field.
overshoot: Three things go past the report. (1) `LiteDB/Document/Expression/Parser/BsonExpressionParser.cs:305` now gates the single-field shortcut on `aliases.Count == 0`, so `SELECT $ AS payload`, `SELECT {a:1} AS payload` and `SELECT EXTEND($, {...}) AS payload` change output shape — the alias used to be ignored and the raw document returned, now the result is nested under the alias. That has nothing to do with ORDER BY and silently changes results for anyone using those forms; `Issue2583NestedAlias_Tests.Single_document_alias_is_projected_and_used_for_ordering` pins the new shape. (2) An alias now shadows a same-named source field in ORDER BY (`SELECT _id, 100 - amount AS rank ... ORDER BY rank` sorts by the computed value, not by the stored `rank`). SQL-standard and there is an escape hatch (`ORDER BY $.rank`), but it is an undocumented silent result change for existing queries. (3) `ResolveSelectAlias` calls `CompileSelectAlias` on both the alias and the whole SELECT projection, deliberately bypassing the compiled-delegate cache — two extra `Expression.Compile` calls on every execution of an alias-ordered query. Only queries that previously did not sort at all pay it, so the cost is contained. The OrdinalIgnoreCase rename (`rank` -> `rank1`) is not overshoot: `BsonDocument` is already OrdinalIgnoreCase, so the old code silently collapsed case-variant aliases.
suggestedAction: Comment on #2583: fixed in PR #2917, both of their queries now sort by the computed value; add one line that when an alias has the same name as a stored field, ORDER BY now picks the alias and `ORDER BY $.fieldname` forces the stored field. Separately, call out the `SELECT $ AS x` / `SELECT EXTEND(...) AS x` projection-shape change in the release notes (or split it into its own commit), since it changes output for queries that never involved ORDER BY.

issueTitle: [BUG] collection.UpdateMany stores property with DbRef inline instead of as reference
reporterNeed: rklfss (LiteDB 5.0.15, confirmed still broken on 6.0.0-prerelease.75) does `db.GetCollection<A>().UpdateMany(x => new A { Id = x.Id, Bref = b2 }, x => x.Id == 11)` where `A.Bref` is `[BsonRef]`. The captured `b2` instance was written inline as `{ "_id": 2 }` instead of `{ "$id": 2, "$ref": "B" }`, silently corrupting the document so later Include/reads fail. They wanted the expression translator to use the destination member's DbRef mapping, not the entity type's own serializer.
whatChanged: `TryVisitDbRefIdExpression` (the only path used by `VisitMemberInit` for DbRef member assignments, LinqExpressionVisitor.cs:430) now calls the new `TryVisitCapturedDbRef` first. For any assignment that has no lambda parameter, no server-runtime node (DateTime.Now/UtcNow/Today, Guid.NewGuid) and no `BsonRefId<T>` marker, it evaluates the expression client-side and serializes it through `memberMapper.Serialize` — the exact delegate `RegisterDbRefItem`/`RegisterDbRefList` installs — then emits the resulting `{$id,$ref[,$type]}` document as a parameter constant. It also extends this to list/array destinations (`VisitDbRefList`, which drops nulls the same way insert-time DbRefList serialization does) and to IIF/COALESCE branches. No production file outside `LiteDB/Client/Mapper/Linq/` is touched; no new public API (`BsonRefId<T>` already shipped in dev via #2741).
gap: In a comment the reporter also raised the row-dependent inline case, `Bref = new B { Id = 100, Name = x.Bref.Name + "_foobar" }`. That still falls through (parameter present → `TrySerializeCapturedDbRef` returns false, `MemberInitExpression` matches no switch case → plain `Visit`) and silently writes an inline document with no `$ref` and no error — the same data-corruption shape the issue is about, just triggered by a different expression. The answer is the `BsonRefId<T>` marker the reporter himself proposed and which now exists, but it is mentioned in no markdown file in the tree (`grep -rl BsonRefId --include=*.md` → nothing), so the reporter has to find it from source.
overshoot: Minor and mostly defensible. (1) A parameter-free inline construction such as `Bref = new B { Id = 100, Name = "x" }` now silently collapses to `{$id:100,$ref:"B"}`, discarding `Name`, where it previously stored the inline document — a silent shape change for anyone who was (incorrectly) relying on the old behaviour. (2) IIF/COALESCE DbRef branch translation is new behaviour the report never asked for. (3) `Evaluate` compiles a lambda per captured DbRef assignment at translation time; negligible, and the same thing already happens for captured members elsewhere (LinqExpressionVisitor.cs:106). No new exception on a previously working path — the list path only relaxes (items that used to throw "not supported for BsonRefId<T>" now serialize), and the `NotSupportedException` for a `[BsonRef]` member with a blank collection name is pre-existing from #2741.
suggestedAction: On merge, reply to rklfss confirming the captured-instance case is fixed, and answer his follow-up explicitly: row-dependent `new B { ... }` inside an update expression is still serialized inline by design, and `new BsonRefId<T>(expr)` — the helper he proposed, now in dev via #2741 — is the supported way to write a computed reference. Worth a short docs section on `BsonRefId<T>`, since it appears in no .md file; optionally a follow-up issue to throw instead of silently inlining a row-dependent `new T{...}` assigned to a `[BsonRef]` member.

issueTitle: [BUG] Opening an encrypted database without a password returns generic ErrorCode 0
reporterNeed: Reporter opens an encrypted file with no password in the connection string and gets `LiteException` with `ErrorCode == 0` and a free-text message, while a wrong password gives `ErrorCode == 217 (INVALID_PASSWORD)`. They cannot programmatically tell this expected password/config failure apart from any other generic LiteDB failure; they asked for either 217 or a new MISSING_PASSWORD code.
whatChanged: `LiteDB/Engine/LiteEngine.cs` Open(): the `buffer[0] == 1` throw now carries `LiteException.INVALID_PASSWORD` instead of `0` (message text unchanged), and the same guarded throw is added on the post-AutoRebuild re-read path (line ~130) where an encrypted buffer previously fell through into `new HeaderPage(buffer)`. Plus a stray BOM removal at the top of the file.
gap: Reuse of 217 means `ErrorCode` alone still cannot separate "no password supplied" from "wrong password" — only the message differs ("This data file is encrypted and needs a password to open" vs "Invalid password."). The reporter explicitly offered this as an acceptable option, so it is a choice rather than a miss, but it is undocumented: nothing in the commit, XML docs, or the issue says 217 was picked over a dedicated MISSING_PASSWORD code.

issueTitle: [BUG] [Crash / unchecked exception] Enum property comparison can abort LINQ translation with EnumAsInteger=false
overshoot:
Two behaviour changes go past the report, both on previously non-crashing paths:
1. EnsureNameStoredEnumOperand now throws NotSupportedException whenever exactly one side of a binary node is an enum conversion chain and the other is a row-dependent non-enum member — including operators that used to translate without crashing, e.g. `x.Id < (int)x.Type` previously emitted `($._id < $.Type)` (number vs stored name: silently wrong/empty) and now throws. Silently-wrong → clear error is defensible, but it is a new exception on a path that used to return results, and no test covers the ordering variant of it.
2. ParameterExpressionVisitor.Test semantics changed globally (lambda-bound parameters no longer count as row dependency). That predicate is consumed at ~20 call sites (captured-member detection, DbRef assignment, Invocation, References, RowText, OrdinalEquals, Enum.Equals), so any expression containing a nested lambda is now classified as closed and locally evaluated where it previously was treated as row-dependent. It is needed to stop the new gating from regressing closed nested lambdas, and only one test (Closed_nested_lambda_remains_a_constant_enum_operand) guards the whole widening.
Also beyond the report, though a straight bug fix: `(Kind)x.Id == Kind.One` with EnumAsInteger=false changes from matching nothing to matching, because GetConvertedEnum now unwraps the cast chain instead of trusting the direct operand type.
reporterNeed: Wwwing301 wanted the ordinary LINQ predicate `p => p.Type == p.BackupType` (two enum properties on the same document) to work with BsonMapper.EnumAsInteger=false. Instead BsonMapper.GetExpression aborted translation with InvalidOperationException "variable 'p' of type 'Phone' referenced from scope '', but it is not defined" before the query ran; the same comparison worked with EnumAsInteger=true and against a constant enum, so they were forced to flip storage format or rewrite the query. No other commenter reports a different problem (the one comment is the maintainer pointing at a fork test fixture).
suggestedAction: Comment on #2770 when the PR lands: state that `==`/`!=` between two enum members now translates under both EnumAsInteger modes, and that `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and arithmetic on name-stored enum members remain unsupported (set EnumAsInteger=true for those). Optional follow-up issue: route the non-equality enum path through the same NotSupportedException message instead of letting Evaluate() surface the raw expression-compiler error, so that case is self-explaining too.
whatChanged: C# compiles enum `==` to `(int)left == (int)right`, and VisitBinary's name-stored-enum branch unconditionally did `Evaluate(node.Right)` — compiling a subtree that still references the query parameter, hence the reporter's exception. The commit gates that branch off for Equal/NotEqual when the right operand is row-dependent (ParameterExpressionVisitor.Test), so `p.Type == p.BackupType` falls through and both Convert nodes are dropped by VisitUnary, emitting `($.Type = $.BackupType)` — a name-to-name comparison that is correct for EnumAsInteger=false. The new EnsureNameStoredEnumOperand rejects the mixed case (enum member vs numeric member) with an actionable NotSupportedException naming EnumAsInteger, and GetConvertedEnum unwraps cast chains so `(Kind)x.Id` is recognised as a number, not an enum.

issueTitle: Index scans and COUNT keep every document address in memory: usage grows ~100 B per document
overshoot: Contained, but not zero. (a) Removing `DistinctBy` for plain reads reopens a window the HashSet used to mask: a read cursor without `ForUpdate` whose caller updates the scanned index key inside an explicit `BeginTrans` now shares the snapshot and can revisit the document (previously deduplicated whenever the update did not relocate the DataBlock). The commit guards `UpdateMany`/`DeleteMany`/SQL `UPDATE`/`ForUpdate()` — all of which set `Query.ForUpdate` — but the manual read-loop-plus-`Update` case is neither covered nor guarded, and the PR body lists it under "pre-existing, not touched". Implicit (query-only) transactions are unaffected because the read snapshot pins `_walIndex.CurrentReadVersion`. (b) The scans now trust the invariant "one node per document in a scalar index"; a physically damaged index holding two nodes for the same DataBlock would surface duplicate rows instead of being silently deduplicated. (c) No public API change: `Index.Run` gains a `bool forUpdate` parameter but `Index`, `IndexVirtual`, `VectorIndexQuery` and `QueryExecutor` are all `internal`. `BsonExpression.CanStreamAggregateSource` is `internal` too. No new exceptions, no changed defaults, no added validation, no per-query cost.
reporterNeed: The reporter (the maintainer himself, writing up a cause found while answering #2266/#2203) wants peak managed memory during a scan to stop growing ~100 B per document, so that `SELECT COUNT(*)`, `col.Count()`, `col.Count(x => x.Flag)` and `col.FindAll().LongCount()` over multi-million-document collections do not consume 1.5 GB at 12M rows or OOM a 32-bit process at 50M. He named the two structures to remove and proposed the exact fix: deduplicate index scans only where duplicates are possible, and let single-pass aggregates stream instead of caching every document address.
suggestedAction: Before closing #2775, add the memory regression the issue itself proposed (or a LiteDB.ReproRunner probe with the numbers recorded in LiteDB-Artifacts), since nothing in the commit demonstrates the 85-130 B/document is gone. In the closing comment state the two residual limits plainly: multi-aggregate selects (`SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(x)`) and GROUP BY still cache one address per document by design, and a plain read cursor that updates the scanned index key inside an explicit transaction without `ForUpdate()` can now revisit documents — either cover that case with a test or document `ForUpdate()` as required for read-then-write loops.
whatChanged: Both structures the issue named are removed for exactly the four queries it measured. `Index.Run` now skips `.DistinctBy(x => x.DataBlock)` when the scan is not a write cursor, the index expression is scalar, and the query is `IndexAll`/`IndexEquals`/`IndexRange`/`IndexScan`/`IndexLike` (`IndexIn` and enumerable `tags[*]` indexes keep deduplicating; I checked `IndexEquals` and `IndexLike.ExecuteStartsWith` and neither re-yields its seed node, so the invariant holds). `QueryPipe.SelectAll` skips `DocumentCacheEnumerable` when the new `BsonExpression.CanStreamAggregateSource` proves the select is scalar and touches the source exactly once. That covers `SELECT COUNT(*)` and, via `LiteQueryable.Count()`'s `{count: COUNT(*._id)}`, both `col.Count()` and `col.Count(x => x.Flag)`; `col.FindAll().LongCount()` gets the `DistinctBy` removal. Safepoints still run — they come from `BasePipe.LoadDocument`, not from the cache — so the bounded page-buffer behaviour is unchanged, and the skipped re-application of INCLUDE in the streaming branch is correct because `Pipe()` already applied IncludeBefore/IncludeAfter to that source. A `forUpdate` flag threaded from `Query.ForUpdate` restores deduplication for write cursors (`UpdateMany`, `DeleteMany`, SQL `UPDATE`, `ForUpdate()`).

gap: Residual, and by design: a call that genuinely touches the row still throws, and the thrown message was shortened to "Method {Name} not available to convert to BsonExpression (...)" — it lost the declaring-type detail the old message carried and still does not hint at the documented workaround (hoist the value into a local). Also unchanged: string.Concat/Format/Join have no server-side translation, so composing row fields (x => x.A + "." + x.B) still fails; #2779 acknowledges that as a TODO rather than fixing it.
issueTitle: LINQ predicates throw on method calls that don't depend on the lambda parameter (string interpolation, Distinct() over a captured list) instead of evaluating them client-side
overshoot: Two items, both minor and neither is the main story. (1) MathResolver.Round now returns null when the second parameter is not int. Closed calls get client-evaluated (correct), but a row-dependent call such as x => Math.Round(x.Value, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero) == 2, which previously emitted ROUND(@0, @1) with the enum landing in the digits slot, now throws NotSupportedException — a new exception on a path that used to execute, and Issue2779_Tests.cs:48-51 pins it. Defensible (the old translation was silently wrong) but it is behaviour no reporter asked about. (2) Closed calls on resolver-owning types are now compiled and invoked once during translation, so user code with side effects runs at query-build time; this only affects expressions that previously threw, so no existing working path regresses. No new public API, no changed defaults, no cost on the mapped/common path (the fallback only runs where an exception was raised before).
reporterNeed: The real reporters are krenukumar (#1294) and juwens (#2219), both closed into this issue. They wanted to run an ordinary LINQ predicate where part of the expression is a plain client-side computation: a captured list's SelectMany(..).Distinct().Contains(x.MobileId), and x.MyStringProperty == $"{strA}.{strB}". LiteDB refused to translate the query at all (NotSupportedException / NotImplementedException from the resolvers), so both had to restructure their code or precompute into a local.
suggestedAction: Nothing blocking. When #2917 ships, post the released version on #1294 and #2219 so the original reporters (krenukumar, juwens) see the close was real, since both were told to "follow #2779" and #2779 itself has no comments. Optionally mention in the release notes that Math.Round(value, MidpointRounding) inside a predicate now throws instead of producing a silently wrong ROUND(x, <enum>).
whatChanged: LinqExpressionVisitor.VisitMethodCall no longer treats "declaring type has a resolver" as a commitment to server-side translation. The resolver lookup and the pre-existing client-eval fallback are merged: if no pattern comes back, a call that touches the lambda parameter throws NotSupportedException, and a call that does not is compiled, executed once and folded into a single @pN parameter. Resolver-mapped methods still translate, so runtime functions such as GUID()/NOW() stay server-side. StringResolver returns null for Format/Join instead of throwing NotImplementedException; MathResolver returns null for Round overloads it cannot express. Concretely: #1294's SelectMany(..).Distinct().Contains(e.MobileId) becomes ITEMS(@p0) ANY=$.MobileId with a filter of $.MobileId IN ARRAY(ITEMS(@p0)), and #2219's interpolated string (which Roslyn lowers to string.Concat/string.Format inside an expression tree) becomes ($.Name=@p0).

gap: Offset is still O(n): the fix removes the document read + BSON deserialize per skipped row but still walks one index node per skipped row. #2092's loop (7M docs, `Limit(10000).Offset(i*10000)`) is still quadratic overall — it gets much faster per chunk but still degrades with i, and that reporter still has to learn on their own that the right answer is a single `FindAll()` enumeration or keyset pagination. Nothing in the commit says so: no docs change, no plan/explain marker, and #2795 is still open with zero comments, so neither #1861 nor #2092 has been given the honest "constant-time offset is out of reach; here is what to do instead" answer their closed issues were redirected here for. Second gap for #1861: their follow-up question ("does it get worse if I add Where()?") now has a non-obvious answer — it is fast only when the optimizer fully consumes the predicate into the index (`query.Filters.Count == 0`); any residual filter or unindexed OrderBy falls back to the old load-then-skip path. That condition is invisible to a user. Their asked-for "query id" continuation handle is not delivered.
issueTitle: Skip/Offset pagination slows down linearly with the offset because skipped documents are fully loaded
overshoot: Essentially none. The change is a single guarded reordering in `QueryPipe.Pipe` (LiteDB/Engine/Query/Pipeline/QueryPipe.cs): no new public API, no new exceptions, no changed defaults, no stricter validation, and the fast path is gated on `Filters.Count == 0 && IncludeBefore.Count == 0 && OrderBy == null` so every other plan keeps its old behaviour. Result sets are unchanged, including the aggregate case (`Select("COUNT(*)").Offset(...)`) and multikey/array indexes, since `LoadDocument` already yielded one document per index node. Extra cost on the new path is one `_transaction.Safepoint()` per skipped node, which was already paid per skipped document before, so it is strictly cheaper. Minor test-side overshoot only: `Issue2795_Tests` reaches into engine internals (`GetMonitor`, `QueryOptimization`, `QueryPipe`, a custom `IDocumentLookup`) and pins optimizer plan shape (`HasResidualFilters`/`IsFullIndexScan` for the `$.sequence >= 1` range case) that the report does not justify — brittle to future optimizer changes, but it harms no user.
reporterNeed: Two consolidated reporters. #1861 (AlBannaTechno, v5.0.9/.NET 4.7.2) paginates a 5,000-row UI list with `col.Query().OrderBy(c => c.PageTitleNumeric).Skip(skip).Limit(take)` on an indexed field; page at Skip(3000) took ~40x the first page. #2092 (eata7) walks ~7M documents in chunks with `collection.Query().Limit(10000).Offset(i*10000)`, where per-chunk time grew from ~0.7s to >15s and memory grew with it. Both want paging that does not get slower as the offset grows; #1861 additionally asked for O(1) access or a reusable "query id" continuation handle.
suggestedAction: Before/when merging, post one comment on #2795 (and it will reach both closed reporters) that says plainly: (1) skipped rows no longer load or deserialize documents, so paged reads are much faster, but offset is still proportional to n — true O(1) offset and a continuation/query-id handle are not coming without a new index structure; (2) the fast path only applies when the query has no residual filter, no Include-before and no leftover OrderBy, i.e. an indexed OrderBy or a predicate the index fully consumes — a `Where()` on an unindexed field still pays the old cost; (3) for #2092's use case the recommended answer is a single `foreach (var doc in col.FindAll())` pass or keyset pagination (`Where("_id > @0", lastId).Limit(k)`), not repeated growing offsets. Land the "recommend keyset pagination for large collections" docs change that the issue's own plan lists and this commit omits.
whatChanged: In `QueryPipe.Pipe`, when the plan has no residual filters, no IncludeBefore and no remaining OrderBy, `Offset` and `Limit` are now applied to the `IndexNode` sequence (new `SkipNodes`, plus `nodes.Take(limit)`) before `LoadDocument`, instead of to already-materialised documents afterwards; `Safepoint()` is called per skipped node to keep the transaction page budget bounded. `DefineOrderBy` already nulls out `OrderBy` when the single sort segment matches the chosen index expression, so #1861's indexed `OrderBy(...).Skip(n)` also lands on the new path. Skipped rows no longer cost a data-block read plus BSON deserialisation — only an index-node read.

gap: No escape syntax and no escaping at the LINQ layer. `StringResolver` still emits `# LIKE ('%' + @0 + '%')` / `('%' + @0)` with the raw user value, and `SqlLike` has no `\%` / `\_`. So: (1) #2728's explicit ask — `EndsWith("_value")` / `LIKE "%_MyValue"` treating `_` as a literal — is unmet; their rows now come back, but so do false positives like "XMyValue", and there is still no way to ask for a literal `_`. Their claimed workaround `"%\_value"` does not work either (backslash is matched literally). (2) A search box passing user text to `Contains` no longer hangs on "%", but still silently gets wildcard semantics with no way to opt out. Also #2728 is currently closed as "Solved in #2727", which the meta-issue itself says was wrong — it is not linked to this fix.
issueTitle: LIKE / LINQ Contains wildcard matching: patterns with consecutive % hang forever and _ after % never matches
overshoot: Small and mostly benign. No new public API, no new exceptions, no changed defaults, no stricter validation. Two things go slightly beyond the listed repros: (a) `SqlLikeStartsWith`'s `hasMore` now returns true when the first wildcard is `_` or when `%` is not the last char, so the indexed StartsWith path runs `SqlLike` on nodes it previously accepted on prefix alone — this is a genuine fix (`"abcdef" LIKE "abc_"` used to return true on an indexed field) but costs one extra matcher call per candidate node for `_`-bearing patterns. (b) The new matcher actually backtracks where the old one bailed out or spun, so pathological patterns ("%a%a%a%b" over long strings) now do real O(n*m) work with the pre-existing per-character `collation.Compare(char.ToString(), char.ToString())` allocations; correct but slower than the old wrong-and-early-exiting path in those cases.
reporterNeed: Issue 2797 is a maintainer-written consolidation of four real user reports. #1883/#2220/#2254 wanted `Contains("01")` / `LIKE '%01%'` to find "001", "26001", "DC00001" (indexed and not). #2728 wanted `LIKE "%_MyValue"` / `EndsWith("_value")` to return their documents, and asked that `_` be treated as a literal. On top of that, any pattern with two consecutive `%` — reachable from LINQ whenever a user types "%" into a search box — spun the CPU forever and never returned.
suggestedAction: Post one comment on #2797 (and reopen or cross-link #2728, which is still closed as "solved by #2727") stating plainly: `%%`, `%_` and the missed-substring cases are fixed by this commit; LIKE still has NO escape syntax and LINQ `Contains`/`StartsWith`/`EndsWith` still splice the raw argument into the pattern, so `_` and `%` in user input remain wildcards — if you need a literal underscore, filter in memory or add the check yourself for now. Track escaping (`\%`, `\_` plus escaping of LINQ-supplied values) as a separate follow-up issue, since that is what #2728 actually asked for. Optionally add one end-to-end test at the LINQ layer (`Where(x => x.Name.Contains("%a0"))` with and without `EnsureIndex`) and a timeout guard, so a reintroduced hang fails CI instead of stalling it.
whatChanged: `StringExtensions.SqlLike` is replaced by the standard greedy two-pointer wildcard matcher (remember the last `%` in pattern and value; on mismatch restart just after that `%` with one more value char consumed; trailing `%` run skipped at the end). Traced by hand, every repro in the issue now gives the right answer and terminates: "001"/"26001"/"DC00001" vs `%01%` → true; `"1aaa0bb0" LIKE "%%a0%"` → true, no hang (the backtrack anchor increases monotonically, so termination is structural); `"0" LIKE "%_"` → true; `"1" LIKE "%_%"` → true; `"b110a1" LIKE "%_1a1"` → false; `"1101" LIKE "1%_0%%"` → true; `"%_MyValue"` now matches. Second change: `SqlLikeStartsWith`'s `hasMore` becomes `i < len && (c != '%' || i < len - 1)`, so a pattern whose first wildcard is `_` (e.g. `"abc_"`) no longer skips the `SqlLike` re-test on the indexed StartsWith path. Tests: a brute-force comparison against an anchored `Regex` oracle over all values of length ≤5 from {a,b} × all patterns of length ≤4 from {a,b,%,_} (this structurally covers `%ab%`, `%_`, `%%`, `a%_b`), plus a `[Theory]` running `"ab_"`, `"a%%b"`, `"a%_b"`, `"%_%"` through `Find` both without and with `EnsureIndex`, again against the regex oracle — so the reporters' scan and index paths are both exercised. Not covered: the literal strings from the reports, the LINQ `Contains`/`EndsWith` translation layer, and any timeout guard (a reintroduced hang would stall CI rather than fail an assertion).

issueTitle: LINQ queries on GetCollection<IInterface> ignore [BsonId] declared on the implementing class and silently match nothing
reporterNeed: The original reporters (#1890 AlBannaTechno, DateTime [BsonId]; #2241 devmaestro1, string [BsonId]) keep the collection typed as an interface (`GetCollection<IFoo>`) while the concrete class carries `[BsonId]`. Insert stores the property as `_id`, but `Find`/`Where`/`DeleteMany` translate the predicate against the interface mapping (`$.Time`, `$.UniqueString`) and silently return/delete nothing, with no exception. They wanted the same predicate to work through the interface as it does through the class.
whatChanged: `LinqExpressionVisitor.ResolveMember` now routes the field name through the new `BsonMapper.ResolveAbstractIdField`. When the member's declaring type is an interface or abstract class with no explicit field/id mapping, it scans already-initialized entity mappers in `_entities` for concrete implementations, matches the declared member to the concrete member via interface maps / virtual base definitions, and, if all known implementations agree, uses their field name (so `d.Time` becomes `$._id`). If the known implementations disagree about whether that member is `_id`, it throws `NotSupportedException`. Supporting plumbing: `MemberMapper.ReflectedMember`/`HasExplicitFieldName` (the public `FieldName` setter now marks the name explicit), `EntityMapper.IsInitialized`/`UsesCustomIdSelection`, and a probe that disables the whole inference when a `BsonMapper` subclass overrides `GetIdMember`.
gap: Inference only fires if the concrete type is already registered in that BsonMapper instance. Registration happens as a side effect of serializing an instance (Insert) or an explicit `mapper.Entity<Concrete>()`. A process that opens an existing file and only queries — `db.GetCollection<IFoo>("x").Find(f => f.UniqueString == "x")` with no prior insert — finds `implementations.Length == 0` and falls straight back to `$.UniqueString`: the same silent empty result, still with no exception and no hint. The commit's own `Issue2798Reopen_Tests` pins exactly this by calling `mapper.Entity<KeyRecord>()` before reopening, i.e. the read-only path needs knowledge the reporter does not have. The issue's option (b) ("detect the mismatch ... instead of silently producing queries that cannot match") is not delivered for this case. Separately, anyone using a `BsonMapper` subclass that overrides `GetIdMember` gets `UsesCustomIdSelection == true` and no fix at all, silently.
overshoot: 1) New exception on paths that worked before. With an abstract base whose `Id` is picked up by convention, `GetCollection<Part>().Find(x => x.Id == 1)` previously resolved to `$._id` and worked. Once a sibling subclass that re-declares its own `[BsonId]` is mapped, the same query now throws `NotSupportedException` — deliberately pinned by `Issue2798InheritedId_Tests.Derived_types_that_really_disagree_on_the_inherited_id_still_throw` and `Issue2798KnownMapping_Tests`. The issue asked for the fallback "only when that mapping is unambiguous", i.e. leave ambiguous cases as they were; throwing is stricter than the report justifies. 2) Because `_entities` is per-mapper and most apps use `BsonMapper.Global`, an implementation registered for a completely different collection can flip an existing query from `$.Key` to `$._id`, or make it throw. 3) Translation now depends on mapper state/ordering: `Initializing_implementation_is_not_waited_on_or_used_for_inference` pins that the same expression yields `$.Key` before the concrete type finishes mapping and `$._id` after. 4) `MemberMapper.FieldName` (public setter) now has the side effect of setting `HasExplicitFieldName`, which changes inference for any code that re-assigns it. 5) Cost: for interface/abstract-declared members the resolution scans all mapped entities and does `GetInterfaceMap`/`GetBaseDefinition` reflection per member per expression translation, with no caching; concrete-typed collections are unaffected (early return).
suggestedAction: Two things, both small: (a) when the declared type is an interface/abstract type with no id mapping and no concrete implementation is known yet, emit the detection the issue asked for (throw or at minimum a clear message naming `mapper.Entity<IFoo>().Id(...)`) instead of silently translating to a field that cannot match — this is the read-only-process case the fix currently misses; (b) reconsider the `NotSupportedException` on disagreement: prefer keeping the pre-change behaviour (fall back to the declared field name) for hierarchies that used to work, or scope the throw to declared types actually used as a collection type, so that registering an unrelated sibling elsewhere in the process cannot break a working query. Then comment on #1890/#2241 confirming their exact repros now work and stating the registration requirement explicitly.

gap: No test goes through the LINQ layer, which is the only API all three original reporters (#1897, #2271, #2408) used. The commit's tests all drive `BsonExpression.Create(...)` string expressions directly. The translation step (`LinqExpressionVisitor.Resolve` building a fresh parameters document per call) is therefore unpinned: a future regression there — or an expression shape LINQ emits that the three tested shapes miss — would not be caught.
